content.question: What is X% of Y?

Read the answer in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.

content.quick_answer: To find a percentage of a number, divide the percent by 100 and multiply by the number. For example, 20% of 100 is 100 × 20 ÷ 100 = 20. Type any percent and any number above and this calculator gives the answer instantly, with the bar and table below showing exactly how the result is made up.
content.formula_words: Percent of a number — in words: divide the percent by 100, then multiply by the whole number.
content.formula_symbol: part = (percent ÷ 100) × whole
content.formula_intro: A percent means “out of 100”, so finding a percent of a number means taking that many hundredths of it:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard arithmetic definition of percent (per hundred). No rate, price or outside data is used by this tool — only the two numbers you type.
example_steps: Start with the percent and the number: 20% of 100.
Turn the percent into a share of 100: 20 ÷ 100 = 0.20.
Multiply the share by the number: 0.20 × 100 = 20.
Answer: 20% of 100 is 20.00 — and what is left of the number is 100 − 20 = 80.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 20 and 100, and the result line shows 20.00.
faqs: How do I work out a percentage of a number by hand?

Divide the percent by 100, then multiply by the number. For example, 20% of 100 is 100 × 20 ÷ 100 = 20. This calculator does the same sum instantly and shows the working in the bar and table under your result.
What is the quick way to find 10% of a number?
10% is one tenth, so divide the number by 10 — or move the decimal point one place to the left. 10% of 250 is 25. From there, 5% is half of that (12.50) and 20% is double it (50).
Can the percent be more than 100?
Yes. A percent over 100 gives an answer bigger than the number itself, because you are taking more than the whole. For example, 150% of 40 is 60, and 200% of 40 is 80 — double the number.
What if the number is zero?

Any percent of 0 is 0.00, and 0% of any number is also 0.00. Those are real answers, not errors, so the calculator shows 0.00. An error only appears if a box is left empty or a number is above the limit.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. For example, 10% of 33.33 is 3.333, which rounds to 3.33. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the breakdown table, so the figures always agree.
Is this calculator free, and do I need to sign up?
Yes, it is free, and no sign-up is needed. Nothing is uploaded: the calculation runs in your browser on your own device, and the numbers you type are not sent anywhere.

content.question: X is what % of Y?

content.quick_answer: To find what percent one number is of another, divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. For example, 45 is what percent of 180? 45 ÷ 180 × 100 = 25%. Type the part and the whole above and the answer appears instantly, with the bar and table below showing how the share is made up.
content.formula_words: What percent one number is of another — in words: divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100.
content.formula_symbol: percent = (part ÷ whole) × 100
content.formula_intro: A percent is a share out of 100, so finding what percent one number is of another means measuring the part against the whole, then scaling that share to hundredths:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard arithmetic definition of percent (per hundred). No rate, price or outside data is used by this tool — only the two numbers you type.
example_steps: Name the part and the whole: part 45, whole 180.
Divide the part by the whole: 45 ÷ 180 = 0.25.
Multiply by 100 to turn the share into a percent: 0.25 × 100 = 25.
Answer: 45 is 25.00% of 180 — and the rest of the whole is 180 − 45 = 135.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 45 and 180, and the result line shows 25.00%.
faqs: How do I work out what percent one number is of another by hand?
Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100. For example, 45 out of 180: 45 ÷ 180 = 0.25, and 0.25 × 100 = 25, so 45 is 25% of 180. This calculator does the same sum instantly as you type.
Can the answer be more than 100%?
Yes, whenever the part is bigger than the whole you compare it with. For example, 150 is 150% of 100, and 90 is 180% of 50. An answer over 100% is a real answer, not an error.
Why does the calculator stop when the whole number is zero?

Because a share of zero cannot be worked out: the sum divides by the whole number, and dividing by zero has no answer in ordinary arithmetic. The calculator shows a clear message instead of a made-up number, and your other entry stays in place so you can fix the zero.
What if the part is zero?

0 is 0.00% of any whole number, because zero is no share at all. That is a real answer, so the calculator shows 0.00% — it only shows an error when the whole number is zero, a box is empty, or a number is above the limit.
How is the answer rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. For example, 1 is 33.333…% of 3, which rounds to 33.33%. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the breakdown table, so the figures always agree.

content.question: Old value → New value: how much change, in percent?
howto: Type the old value and the new value in the boxes. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the answer in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.
Check the bar and table under the result (Part 5 below) to see how the change is made up.
content.quick_answer: To find percentage increase or decrease, subtract the old value from the new value, divide the difference by the old value, and multiply by 100. For example, from 80 to 100 the difference is 20, and 20 ÷ 80 × 100 = +25%, an increase. Type both values above and the change appears instantly below.
content.formula_words: Percentage change — in words: subtract the old value from the new value, divide the difference by the old value, then multiply by 100.
content.formula_symbol: change % = ((new − old) ÷ old) × 100
content.formula_intro: Percentage change measures a difference against the value you started from, then scales it to hundredths. A positive result is an increase; a negative result is a decrease:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard arithmetic definition of percent (per hundred). No rate, price or outside data is used by this tool — only the two numbers you type.
example_steps: Start with the two values: old 80, new 100.
Find the difference: 100 − 80 = 20.
Divide the difference by the old value: 20 ÷ 80 = 0.25.
Multiply by 100: 0.25 × 100 = 25 — the result is positive, so it is an increase.
Answer: from 80 to 100 is an increase of +25.00%.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 80 and 100, and the result line shows +25.00%.
faqs: How do I work out percentage increase by hand?

Subtract the old value from the new value, divide the difference by the old value, then multiply by 100. From 80 to 100: the difference is 20, 20 ÷ 80 = 0.25, and 0.25 × 100 = +25% increase. This calculator does the same sum instantly.
How do I work out percentage decrease?

Use the same formula — the result simply comes out negative. From 100 down to 80: the difference is −20, −20 ÷ 100 = −0.20, and −0.20 × 100 = −20% decrease. The calculator shows the minus sign and the word “decrease” for you.
Why is going from 80 to 100 a 25% rise, but going back from 100 to 80 only a 20% fall?

Because the change is always measured against the value you start from. Going up, the difference of 20 is measured against 80, giving 25%. Coming back down, the same difference of 20 is measured against 100, giving 20%. The starting value is the base, so the two percentages differ.
What is the difference between percentage change and percentage points?

Percentage points is the plain difference between two percentages: 40% to 45% is a rise of 5 percentage points. Percentage change measures that rise against the starting value: 5 ÷ 40 × 100 = 12.50% increase. They are different numbers, so this page always labels which one it shows.
Can a decrease be more than 100%?

Not with ordinary positive values. Falling all the way to zero is a decrease of exactly 100%, and a value cannot fall below zero and stay a normal price, count or measurement. Increases have no such cap: a value that triples has risen by 200%.
What if the old value is zero?

The change cannot be worked out from a starting value of zero, because the formula divides by the old value and dividing by zero has no answer. The calculator shows a clear message instead of a made-up number. If something grew from nothing, describe it with the actual values rather than a percentage.

content.question: What is the price after the discount?
howto: Type the full price and the discount percent in the boxes. There is no Calculate button — the sale price appears as you type.
Read the sale price in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.
Check the bar and table under the result (Part 5 below) to see the full price, the amount saved and the sale price.
content.quick_answer: To work out a sale price, find the amount saved and take it off the full price. For example, 25% off 80 saves 20, so the sale price is 60. Type any price and discount percent above and this calculator gives the sale price and the amount saved instantly, with the breakdown below.
content.formula_words: Sale price — in words: take the discount percent of the price, then subtract that saving from the price.
content.formula_symbol: sale price = price − (price × discount ÷ 100)
content.formula_intro: A discount is a share of the price taken off, so the sale price is what is left after that share is removed:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard arithmetic definition of percent. No rate, price or outside data is used by this tool — only the two numbers you type, in your own currency.
example_steps: Start with the price and the discount: price 80, discount 25%.
Work out the saving: 80 × 25 ÷ 100 = 20.
Take the saving off the price: 80 − 20 = 60.
Answer: the sale price is 60.00, and you save 20.00.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 80 and 25, and the result line shows 60.00.
faqs: How do I work out a discount by hand?

Multiply the price by the discount percent and divide by 100 to get the saving, then subtract the saving from the price. For 25% off 80: 80 × 25 ÷ 100 = 20 saved, so 80 − 20 = 60. This calculator does the same sum instantly.
What is 20% off 50?
20% of 50 is 10, so the sale price is 50 − 10 = 40. A quick check: 10% of 50 is 5, so 20% is double that, 10.
Can the discount be more than 100%?

No. A discount over 100% would make the sale price negative, which has no meaning for a price, so this calculator does not accept a discount above 100%. A discount of 100% makes the item free: the sale price is 0.00.
What is the difference between a discount and a sale price?

The discount is the amount taken off, and the sale price is what you actually pay. On an 80 item with 25% off, the discount is 20 and the sale price is 60. This page shows both, so you can see each one.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. For example, 50% off 49.99 is 24.995, which rounds to 24.99. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the table, so the figures always agree.
Does the discount include tax?

No. This tool works on the price you type, before or after tax, exactly as you type it. If the price on the shelf already includes tax, type that price; if you want the price before tax, work it out on the VAT calculator first.

content.question: How much VAT is on this price?

fields.label: What the price is
options: Price with VAT — take VAT out

howto: Type the price and the VAT rate, then pick whether the price is without VAT or with VAT already in it. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the answer in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.
Check the bar and table under the result (Part 5 below) to see the net price, the VAT and the gross price.
content.quick_answer: To add VAT, multiply the price by the VAT rate and add it on: 20% VAT on 100 is 20, so the price with VAT is 120. To take VAT out of a price that already includes it, divide by one plus the rate. Pick the direction above for the net price, the VAT and the gross price instantly.
content.formula_words: VAT — in words: to add VAT, take the rate percent of the net price and add it on; to remove VAT, divide the gross price by one plus the rate.
content.formula_symbol: VAT = net × rate ÷ 100, and gross = net + VAT; net = gross ÷ (1 + rate ÷ 100)
content.formula_intro: VAT is a percent added to a net price. The direction matters: adding VAT and removing VAT are different sums, so pick the right one first:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard arithmetic of value added tax. The VAT rate is typed by you, because rates differ by country and by item — this site does not guess your rate. Amounts are in your own currency.
example_steps: Start with the net price and the rate: price 100, VAT rate 20%, adding VAT.
Work out the VAT: 100 × 20 ÷ 100 = 20.
Add the VAT to the net price: 100 + 20 = 120.
Answer: the price with VAT is 120.00, and the VAT is 20.00.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 100 and 20 with “Price without VAT” picked, and the result line shows 120.00. Switch to “Price with VAT” and type 120 to see the VAT taken back out.
faqs: How do I add VAT to a price?

Multiply the price by the VAT rate and divide by 100, then add that VAT to the price. At 20% on 100, the VAT is 20 and the price with VAT is 120. Pick “Price without VAT” above and the calculator does it for you.
How do I take VAT out of a price?
Divide the price by one plus the rate as a share. At 20% VAT, divide by 1.20: a price of 120 with VAT in it is 120 ÷ 1.20 = 100 without VAT, so the VAT inside is 20. Pick “Price with VAT” above.
Why is the VAT inside 120 not 24?

Because 20% VAT is worked out on the net price of 100, not on the gross price of 120. The VAT inside a price that already includes 20% VAT is one sixth of it: 120 ÷ 6 = 20. Taking 20% off the gross price is a common mistake.
What VAT rate should I type?

Type the rate that applies to your item in your country — for example 20% is the standard rate in the UK, but food, books and other items can carry a lower rate. This site does not know your item or your country, so it never guesses a rate for you.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. For example, taking 20% VAT out of 99 gives a net price of 82.50. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the table, so the figures always agree.
Is the VAT shown here what I pay at the till?

Only if the price and rate you typed are the ones that apply. The tool does the arithmetic exactly; whether the rate is right for your item is something to check against the seller or your tax authority.

content.question: What is my monthly mortgage payment?
howto: Pick your country first — it changes the currency symbol and the note under the result. Then type the loan amount, the yearly interest rate and the term in years. There is no Calculate button — the payment appears as you type.
Read the monthly payment in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.
Check the bar and table under the result (Part 5 below) to see the total interest and the total paid over the whole term.
content.quick_answer: A monthly mortgage payment comes from the loan amount, the yearly interest rate and the term. For example, a loan of 200,000 at 5% a year over 25 years costs about 1,169.18 a month. Type your own loan, rate and term above and this calculator gives the monthly payment, the total interest and the total paid.
content.formula_words: Monthly mortgage payment — in words: take the monthly interest rate, multiply it by the loan, and divide by one minus the monthly rate factor raised to the number of months.
content.formula_symbol: M = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), where r is the monthly rate and n is the number of months
content.formula_intro: A mortgage is repaid in equal monthly payments that cover interest and part of the loan. The standard repayment formula is:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard amortisation formula for a fixed-rate repayment loan. The interest rate is typed by you — this site does not fetch live mortgage rates. This is an estimate only, not professional advice.
example_steps: Start with the loan, rate and term: loan 200,000, yearly rate 5%, term 25 years (300 months).
Work out the monthly rate: 5 ÷ 100 ÷ 12 = 0.004167.
Answer: the monthly payment is £1,169.18. Over 300 months that is £350,754.02 in total, of which £150,754.02 is interest.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 200000, 5 and 25 with United Kingdom picked, and the result line shows £1,169.18. Change the country to see the same payment in dollars.
faqs: What does the monthly payment include?
Only the loan repayment and the interest on it. It does not include property tax, home insurance, mortgage insurance or lender fees, which are charged separately in most countries.
What happens if the interest rate changes?
The payment changes with it. A higher rate means a higher monthly payment and more total interest; a lower rate means the opposite. Type the new rate above to see the new payment at once.
Does a longer term mean a lower payment?

Yes, the monthly payment falls, because the loan is spread over more months — but the total interest rises, because you pay interest for longer. Compare 25 years with 30 years above to see both effects.
Why is the total interest so large?

Because interest is charged on the amount still owed every month, and a mortgage runs for decades. On a 200,000 loan at 5% over 25 years, the interest is about 150,755 — roughly three quarters of the loan again.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. Each line is rounded on its own for display, so multiplying the rounded monthly payment by the number of months can differ by a few cents from the total shown.
Is this the payment my bank will charge?
Not exactly. Banks round payments their own way, add fees, and may use a different day count. Use this figure to plan and compare; ask your lender for the exact payment before you sign anything.

What is the effective yearly rate?

Is tax taken off the interest here?

What if the interest rate is zero?

content.quick_answer: The yearly yield, or APY, is the real yearly growth of a rate once compounding is counted. A nominal rate of 5% a year compounded monthly is really 5.12% a year, because each month's interest earns interest too. Type any nominal rate and compounding choice above and this calculator gives the APY instantly.
content.formula_words: Annual percentage yield — in words: divide the nominal rate by the number of times interest is added a year, add one, raise it to that number, and subtract one.

faqs: What is the difference between a nominal rate and APY?

The nominal rate is the rate before compounding is counted; the APY is the real yearly growth after compounding. A 5% nominal rate compounded monthly is really 5.12% a year. When the rate compounds once a year, the two are the same.
Why does compounding more often raise the APY?

Because interest is added sooner, so it starts earning interest of its own sooner. At a 6% nominal rate, the APY is 6.00% compounded once a year, 6.09% twice a year, 6.14% four times a year and 6.17% monthly.
Which number should I compare when choosing an account?
Compare the APY, not the nominal rate. Two accounts can quote the same nominal rate but pay different APYs if one compounds monthly and the other once a year. The APY is the fair comparison.
Can the APY be lower than the nominal rate?
No. Compounding only ever adds to the growth, so the APY is always the nominal rate or higher. The two are equal only when interest is added once a year.
Does APY include tax or fees?
No. The figures are before any tax on interest and before any account fees. Your bank can tell you what tax and fees apply to your account.
How is the APY rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. For example, a 5% nominal rate compounded monthly gives an APY of 5.12%. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the table, so the figures always agree.

content.quick_answer: Take-home pay in the USA is your salary less federal income tax and FICA, which is Social Security and Medicare. For example, a single filer on 60,000 in 2026 keeps about 50,390 a year after 5,020 of federal tax and 4,590 of FICA. Type your salary and filing status above for your own figure, with state tax not included.

This is an estimate only, not professional advice.Federal brackets (single, 2026): 10% to $12,400; 12% to $50,400; 22% to $105,700; 24% to $201,775; 32% to $256,225; 35% to $640,600; 37% above. example_steps: Start with the salary and status: 60,000, single. The standard deduction is 16,100, so the taxable income is 60,000 − 16,100 = 43,900.
Work out the federal tax: 10% of 12,400 is 1,240, plus 12% of (43,900 − 12,400) = 3,780, so the federal tax is 5,020.00.
Work out FICA: Social Security 6.2% of 60,000 is 3,720, and Medicare 1.45% of 60,000 is 870, so FICA is 4,590.00.
Answer: the take-home pay is 60,000 − 5,020.00 − 4,590.00 = $50,390.00 a year, or $4,199.17 a month.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 60000 with Single picked, and the result line shows $50,390.00.
faqs: Is state income tax included?
No. State tax rates differ by state, and some states charge no income tax at all, so this page covers federal tax and FICA only. Check your state rate separately and take it off the figure here.
What is FICA?

FICA is the payroll tax on your wages: Social Security at 6.2% up to the 2026 wage base of $184,500, and Medicare at 1.45% on all wages, plus an extra 0.9% of Medicare on wages over $200,000 for a single filer or $250,000 for a married couple filing jointly.
What is the standard deduction?

It is the amount taken off your salary before any tax is worked out: $16,100 for a single filer, $32,200 for a married couple filing jointly and $24,150 for a head of household in 2026. If you itemise deductions instead, this page does not cover that.
Why is my take-home pay lower than my salary divided by 12?
Because tax and FICA come off first. On a $60,000 salary the monthly take-home pay is $4,199.17, not $5,000, because $5,020 of federal tax and $4,590 of FICA come off over the year.
Does this include 401(k) or health insurance taken from my pay?

No. Retirement contributions, health insurance premiums and any other payroll deductions are not included, because they differ from person to person. Take them off the take-home pay shown here yourself.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. Each line — federal tax, Social Security and Medicare — is rounded to cents first, and the take-home pay is the salary less those rounded lines, so the figures always agree.

It is a 2% levy on taxable income that helps pay for Medicare, Australia's public health system. Low-income earners pay less: nothing under $28,011 in 2026-27, then a reduced amount until the full 2% applies at $35,014.
Is super taken out of my take-home pay?

No. The Superannuation Guarantee of 12% is paid by your employer into your super fund on top of your salary. On an 80,000 salary that is 9,600 a year of super, and your take-home pay is worked out before it.
Are HECS-HELP repayments included?

No. Study loan repayments are taken from your pay on top of tax, at rates that depend on your income, so they are not included here. Take them off the take-home pay shown here yourself if they apply to you.

It is not included. The offset reduces tax for lower incomes, so this page can overstate the tax a little for salaries under about $66,667. The page says so plainly: no offsets are claimed here.

example_steps: Start with the salary and code: 35,000, tax code 1257, so the personal allowance is 1257 × 10 = 12,570.
Work out the taxable income: 35,000 − 12,570 = 22,430.

faqs: What is the personal allowance?
It is the amount you can earn before any income tax is due: £12,570 in 2026/27. It comes from your tax code number times £10, so code 1257L gives 1257 × £10 = £12,570.
What happens to the allowance over £100,000?
It falls by £1 for every £2 you earn over £100,000, and it is gone entirely by £125,140. On a salary of £120,000 with code 1257L, the allowance is only £2,570.
What does marginal mean?
Each tax rate applies only to the slice of taxable income inside its band. Moving into the 40% band does not mean you pay 40% on all your income — only the slice above £50,270 is taxed at 40%.
Does this cover Scotland?
No. Scotland sets its own income tax bands for non-savings income, so this page uses the England, Wales and Northern Ireland bands. The personal allowance is the same UK-wide.
Does this include National Insurance?
No. National Insurance is a separate contribution taken from your pay. To see your take-home pay after both income tax and National Insurance, use the UK take-home pay calculator.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. The tax is rounded to cents, and the monthly figure is the yearly tax divided by 12, rounded the same way, so the figures always agree.

What changed in 2026?
The lowest federal rate fell from 15% to 14% for the full year, and the brackets rose by 2% for inflation. The basic personal amount rose to $16,452. This page uses the 2026 figures.
What does marginal mean?
Each tax rate applies only to the slice of income inside its bracket. Moving into the 20.5% bracket does not mean you pay 20.5% on all your income — only the slice above $58,523 is taxed at 20.5%.
Is provincial tax included?

content.question: What is my Body Mass Index (BMI)?
howto: Pick metric or imperial first, then type your weight and height in those units. There is no Calculate button — your BMI appears as you type.
Read the BMI in the result line, rounded half-up to 1 decimal place, with the weight category under it.
Check the bar and table under the result (Part 5 below) to see the healthy weight range for your height.
content.quick_answer: Body Mass Index is your weight divided by your height squared. For example, 70 kilograms at 175 centimetres gives a BMI of 22.9, which is in the healthy weight range. Type your weight and height above, in metric or imperial units, and this calculator gives your BMI, its category and the healthy weight range for your height.
content.formula_words: BMI — in words: divide your weight in kilograms by your height in metres, squared. In imperial units, multiply your weight in pounds by 703 and divide by your height in inches, squared.
content.formula_symbol: BMI = weight in kg ÷ (height in m)², or BMI = 703 × weight in lb ÷ (height in in)²
content.formula_intro: BMI compares weight with height, so taller people are not judged by the same weight as shorter people. The formula is:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard Body Mass Index definition (weight divided by height squared), with the World Health Organization category cut-offs: under 18.5 underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 healthy weight, 25 to 29.9 overweight, 30 and over obesity. This is a guide only, not medical advice.
example_steps: Start with the figures: weight 70 kg, height 175 cm.
Turn the height into metres: 175 cm = 1.75 m, and square it: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625.
Divide the weight by that number: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.857.
Answer: the BMI is 22.9, which is in the healthy weight range (18.5 to 24.9).
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 70 and 175 with Metric picked, and the result line shows 22.9.
faqs: What is a healthy BMI?
A BMI from 18.5 to 24.9 is classed as a healthy weight. Under 18.5 is underweight, 25 to 29.9 is overweight, and 30 and over is obesity. These are the World Health Organization cut-offs for adults.
Is BMI the same for everyone?

No. BMI does not measure body fat, muscle or bone, so it can mislead for athletes with a lot of muscle, older people, children and pregnant women. For children, BMI is judged against growth charts, not the adult cut-offs.
How do I work out BMI in pounds and inches?

Multiply your weight in pounds by 703, then divide by your height in inches squared. For example, 154 lb at 69 in: 703 × 154 ÷ (69 × 69) = 22.7. Pick Imperial above and the calculator does it for you.
What weight is healthy for my height?
Multiply 18.5 and 24.9 by your height in metres squared. At 175 cm that is 56.7 to 76.3 kg. The table under your result shows the range for the height you typed.
Can BMI tell me if I am healthy?

Not on its own. BMI is one rough guide to weight for height. Blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, fitness and how you feel all matter too. If your BMI is outside the healthy range, talk to a doctor rather than acting on this number alone.
How is the BMI rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 1 decimal place. For example, 70 kg at 175 cm gives 22.857, which rounds to 22.9. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the table, so the figures always agree.

content.question: How many calories do I need a day (TDEE)?

fields.label: Activity level
options: Lightly active — light exercise 1 to 3 days a week
Moderately active — exercise 3 to 5 days a week
Very active — hard exercise 6 to 7 days a week
Extra active — physical job or training twice a day

howto: Type your weight, height and age, pick your sex and your activity level. There is no Calculate button — your daily calories appear as you type.
Read the daily calorie need in the result line, as a whole number of calories a day.
Check the bar and table under the result (Part 5 below) to see your resting burn and what to eat to lose or gain weight slowly.
content.quick_answer: Your daily calorie need, or TDEE, is the calories you burn at rest plus the calories your activity adds. For example, a 30-year-old man of 70 kg and 175 cm who exercises 3 to 5 days a week needs about 2,556 calories a day. Type your own figures above and this calculator gives your daily need.
content.formula_words: TDEE — in words: work out your resting burn from your weight, height, age and sex, then multiply it by your activity factor.
content.formula_symbol: TDEE = BMR × activity factor, where BMR = 10 × weight + 6.25 × height − 5 × age + 5 for men or − 161 for women
content.formula_intro: The resting burn (BMR) comes from the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, and the activity factor scales it up to a full day:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the Mifflin-St Jeor equation (1990) for basal metabolic rate, with the standard activity factors 1.2, 1.375, 1.55, 1.725 and 1.9. This is a guide only, not medical advice and not a diet plan.
content.example_title: Worked example: man, 30 years, 70 kg, 175 cm, moderately active
example_steps: Start with the figures: weight 70 kg, height 175 cm, age 30, male, activity factor 1.55.
Work out the resting burn: 10 × 70 + 6.25 × 175 − 5 × 30 + 5 = 1,648.75, which rounds to 1,649 calories a day.
Multiply by the activity factor: 1,648.75 × 1.55 = 2,555.56, which rounds to 2,556.
Answer: the daily calorie need (TDEE) is about 2,556 calories a day.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 70, 175 and 30 with Male and “Moderately active” picked, and the result line shows 2,556.
faqs: What is TDEE?

Total Daily Energy Expenditure: all the calories you burn in a day, including your resting burn, moving around, exercise and digesting food. Eat about your TDEE to stay the same weight, less to lose weight and more to gain weight.
What is BMR?

Basal Metabolic Rate: the calories your body burns at complete rest, just to keep you alive — breathing, keeping warm and running your organs. It is the biggest part of your TDEE, and the BMR calculator on this site works it out on its own.
How do I pick my activity level?

Be honest about a normal week. Desk job with almost no exercise is sedentary (1.2); light exercise 1 to 3 days a week is lightly active (1.375); exercise 3 to 5 days a week is moderately active (1.55). Picking a higher level than you really do is the most common mistake.
How many fewer calories should I eat to lose weight?

About 500 fewer a day loses roughly half a kilogram a week for most people. The table under your result shows your TDEE less 500. Losing weight faster than that is hard to keep up and is best talked through with a doctor.
Is this a diet plan?

No. It is a guide to how many calories your body uses. What you eat, your health and any medical conditions all matter too. If you have a medical condition or take medicine, talk to a doctor before changing what you eat.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: whole numbers, no decimal places. The resting burn is rounded to a whole calorie first, and the daily need is the resting burn times the activity factor, rounded to a whole calorie, so the figures always agree.

content.quick_answer: Your basal metabolic rate, or BMR, is the calories your body burns at complete rest, just to keep you alive. For example, a 30-year-old man of 70 kg and 175 cm burns about 1,649 calories a day at rest. Type your weight, height, age and sex above and this calculator gives your BMR instantly.
content.formula_words: BMR — in words: take ten times your weight in kilograms, add six and a quarter times your height in centimetres, subtract five times your age, then add five for men or subtract 161 for women.
content.formula_symbol: BMR = 10 × weight + 6.25 × height − 5 × age + 5 for men, or − 161 for women
content.formula_intro: The Mifflin-St Jeor equation is the most widely used way to estimate resting burn from body measurements:

faqs: What is BMR?

Basal Metabolic Rate: the calories your body burns at complete rest, just to stay alive — breathing, keeping warm and running your organs. It does not include moving around, exercise or digesting food.
Is BMR the same as my daily calorie need?

No. Your daily need, or TDEE, is your BMR times an activity factor, because moving around and exercise burn more on top. The table under your result shows your daily need at three activity levels, and the TDEE calculator on this site works it out in full.
Why is BMR lower for women?

On average, women carry less muscle and more body fat than men of the same weight and height, and muscle burns more calories at rest than fat. The equation allows for that with a different constant: plus 5 for men, minus 161 for women.
Does BMR change with age?
Yes, it falls slowly as you get older, because muscle is lost and the body uses less energy at rest. The equation subtracts 5 calories a day for every year of age.
Can I raise my BMR?

Building muscle raises it a little, because muscle burns more calories at rest than fat. But the change is small next to the calories burned by moving and exercising, so activity matters far more than BMR alone.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: whole numbers, no decimal places. The BMR is rounded to a whole calorie, and the daily needs in the table are that rounded BMR times each activity factor, rounded to whole calories, so the figures always agree.

content.question: How old am I exactly?
howto: Pick your date of birth from the calendar box, then pick the date to measure to — usually today. There is no Calculate button — your exact age appears as you type.
Read your age in the result line, in years, months and days.
Check the bar and table under the result (Part 5 below) to see the total months, weeks and days.
content.quick_answer: Your exact age is the time from your date of birth to the date you measure to, counted in years, months and days. For example, someone born on 15 June 1990 is 36 years, 4 months and 27 days old on 11 November 2026. Pick both dates above and this calculator gives your exact age instantly.
content.formula_words: Age — in words: count the full years from your birth date to the measuring date, then the full months left over, then the days left over.
content.formula_symbol: age = full years, then full months, then days, from the birth date to the measuring date
content.formula_intro: Age is counted in whole calendar years, months and days, not by dividing the total days by 365, because months and years are not all the same length:
content.formula_source: Formula source: calendar arithmetic on the dates you type, counting full years and months on the calendar, leap years included. Dates from 1900 onwards are accepted.
content.example_title: Worked example: born 15 June 1990, measured on 11 November 2026
example_steps: Start with the two dates: birth 15 June 1990, measuring date 11 November 2026.
Count the full years: from 15 June 1990 to 15 June 2026 is 36 years.
Count the full months left: from 15 June 2026 to 15 October 2026 is 4 months, and from 15 October to 11 November is 27 days.
Answer: the age is 36 years, 4 months, 27 days — 13,298 days in total.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: pick 15 June 1990 and 11 November 2026, and the result line shows 36 years, 4 months, 27 days.
faqs: Why is my age in months and days, not just years?
Because two people born in the same year can be months apart in age. Years, months and days give the exact age on the measuring date, which is what forms, schools and official records ask for.
Does the calculator count leap years?

Yes. The count runs on the real calendar, so 29 February is counted in leap years. Someone born on 29 February 2000 is 26 years old on 28 February 2026 and turns 27 on 1 March 2026 in most legal counting, because there is no 29 February in 2026.
Can I work out my age on a past or future date?
Yes. Pick any measuring date on or after your birth date, in 1900 or later. For example, pick the date of a wedding or a deadline to see how old you will be then.
What if the birth date is after the measuring date?
That has no meaning as an age, so the calculator shows a clear message instead of a result. Pick a birth date on or before the measuring date.
How is the total in days worked out?
It is the plain count of days between the two dates, leap days included. From 15 June 1990 to 11 November 2026 that is 13,298 days.
How are the answers rounded?
Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: whole numbers, no decimal places. Years, months, days and totals are all whole counts, so there is nothing to round.

Read the days between the dates in the result line, as a whole number of days.

content.quick_answer: This page does two date jobs at once. It counts the days between two dates — for example, 30 days lie between 11 November 2026 and 11 December 2026 — and it works out the date a number of days before or after a date. Pick the dates and type the days above, and both answers appear.
content.formula_words: Days between dates — in words: count the days from the first date to the second on the calendar, leap days included. To add days, move forward on the calendar; to subtract days, move back.
content.formula_symbol: days between = second date − first date, in days; new date = first date ± days
content.formula_intro: Dates are counted on the real calendar, so month lengths and leap years are handled exactly:
content.formula_source: Formula source: calendar arithmetic on the dates you type, leap years included. Dates from 1900 to 2100 are accepted.
example_steps: Start with the dates: first date 11 November 2026, second date 11 December 2026, and 30 days to add.
Count the days between the two dates: from 11 November to 11 December is 30 days.
Add 30 days to the first date: 11 November plus 30 days is 11 December 2026.
Answer: there are 30 days between the dates, and 30 days after 11 November 2026 is 11 December 2026.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: pick 11 November 2026 and 11 December 2026 with 30 days, and the result line shows 30 days.
faqs: Does the count include the start and end dates?
No. The count is the days from the first date to the second, so 11 November to 11 December is 30 days, not 31. If you need both end dates counted, add 1 to the answer.
Does the calculator handle leap years?
Yes. February has 29 days in leap years, so 28 February 2024 to 1 March 2024 is 2 days, while in a non-leap year it is 1 day.
Can I count days between past dates?
Yes. Pick any two dates between 1900 and 2100, in either order — the count is always the number of days between them, and it is never negative.
How do I work out a deadline 30 days from now?
Pick the start date, type 30, and pick “After the first date”. The table under the result shows the date 30 days after, and the date 30 days before, the first date.
What is the most days I can add?
36,500 days, which is about 100 years. Adding more than that is not accepted, because the result would fall outside the 1900 to 2100 range this page covers.
How are the answers rounded?
Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: whole numbers, no decimal places. Days and dates are whole counts, so there is nothing to round.

Read the time between the two times in the result line, in hours and minutes.

content.quick_answer: This page does two time jobs at once. It counts the time between two times — for example, 8 hours 15 minutes lie between 09:30 and 17:45 — and it adds or subtracts hours and minutes from a time. Pick the times and type the hours and minutes above, and both answers appear with the working shown.
content.formula_words: Time between two times — in words: turn both times into minutes after midnight, subtract, and turn the answer back into hours and minutes. To add or subtract, add or take away the minutes and wrap past midnight if needed.
content.formula_symbol: duration = end time − start time, in minutes; new time = start time ± hours and minutes
content.formula_intro: Times are worked out in minutes after midnight, so the sums are plain subtraction and addition:
content.formula_source: Formula source: time arithmetic on the times you type, on a 24-hour clock. Hours run 0 to 23 and minutes run 0 to 59. If the end time is earlier than the start time, it is counted as the next day.
example_steps: Start with the times: start 09:30, end 17:45.
Turn both into minutes after midnight: 09:30 is 570 minutes, 17:45 is 1,065 minutes.
Subtract: 1,065 − 570 = 495 minutes, which is 8 hours 15 minutes.
Answer: the time between 09:30 and 17:45 is 8 hours 15 minutes. Adding 2 hours 30 minutes to 09:30 gives 12:00.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: pick 09:30 and 17:45 with 2 hours and 30 minutes to add, and the result line shows 8 hours 15 minutes.
faqs: What if the end time is earlier than the start time?
It is counted as the next day. From 22:00 to 06:30 is 8 hours 30 minutes, because the end time falls on the next day. This is the usual way night shifts are counted.
How do I add hours to a time?
Type the hours and minutes and pick “Add to the start time”. The table under the result shows the start time plus the hours and minutes, wrapping past midnight: 23:30 plus 2 hours is 01:30.
Does this count seconds?
No. This page works in hours and minutes only, which is what work shifts, school days and travel times are usually counted in. Seconds are not accepted.
Can I work out a shift length that crosses midnight?
Yes. Pick the start time and the end time, and the page counts the end time as the next day when it is earlier. A shift from 22:00 to 06:30 is 8 hours 30 minutes.
Why is the answer in hours and minutes, not a decimal?
Because 8.25 hours is harder to read as a time than 8 hours 15 minutes. The table shows the answer the same way, so the figures always agree.
How are the answers rounded?
Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: whole numbers, no decimal places. Hours and minutes are whole counts, so there is nothing to round.

content.quick_answer: This calculator works out sums with brackets, powers, roots, logs and trig, all in one box. For example, 2+3*4 is 14, because multiplication comes before addition, and sin(30) is 0.5. Type any sum above, or tap the keys, and the answer appears instantly, with a clear message if the sum cannot be read.
content.formula_words: Scientific calculator — in words: work out brackets first, then powers and roots, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Trig works in degrees, log is base 10, ln is the natural log, and % after a number means percent.
content.formula_intro: The calculator reads your sum the way maths is written, with the usual order of operations:
content.formula_source: Formula source: standard arithmetic and the standard maths functions (sin, cos, tan, log base 10, natural log, square root, powers). Angles are in degrees, as on most pocket calculators. No data is fetched and nothing is stored.
example_steps: Start with the sum: 2 + 3 × 4.
Work out the multiplication first: 3 × 4 = 12.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 2+3*4, and the result line shows 14. Try sqrt(16)+2^3 for 12, or sin(30) for 0.5.
faqs: What order does the calculator work sums out in?
Brackets first, then powers and roots, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. So 2+3*4 is 14, not 20, and (2+3)*4 is 20. Use brackets whenever the order is not clear.
Are angles in degrees or radians?
Degrees, as on most pocket calculators. sin(30) is 0.5, sin(90) is 1 and cos(60) is 0.5. If you need radians, the inverse functions (asin, acos, atan) give their answers in degrees too.
What does % do in a sum?
It means percent: 50% is 0.5, so 200*50% is 100. It is not the remainder operation that some programming languages use.
How do I type a power or a root?
Use ^ for a power: 2^3 is 8, and 2^-1 is 0.5. Use sqrt( for a square root: sqrt(16) is 4. Use log( for base 10 and ln( for the natural log: log(100) is 2 and ln(10) is about 2.302585093.
What if my sum cannot be worked out?

The calculator shows a clear message instead of a made-up number: a missing bracket, a word it does not know, dividing by zero, a log of zero or less, or a square root of a negative number all give a message that says what is wrong.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 10 decimal places, with trailing zeros cut off. For example, sin(30) is 0.5, not 0.5000000000. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the table, so the figures always agree.

content.question: What is the answer to this fraction sum?
howto: Type the two fractions as top and bottom numbers, then pick add, subtract, multiply or divide. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the answer in the result line as a simplified fraction, with the decimal under it.
Check the bar and table under the result (Part 5 below) to see both fractions, the answer and the decimal.
content.quick_answer: To add or subtract fractions, give them the same bottom number, then add or subtract the top numbers; to multiply, multiply straight across; to divide, flip the second fraction and multiply. For example, 1/2 + 1/3 is 5/6. Type both fractions above and this calculator gives the simplified answer and the decimal.
content.formula_words: Fraction sums — in words: to add or subtract, use a common bottom number; to multiply, multiply the tops and the bottoms; to divide, turn the second fraction upside down and multiply.
content.formula_symbol: a/b + c/d = (a×d + c×b) ÷ (b×d); a/b × c/d = (a×c) ÷ (b×d); a/b ÷ c/d = (a×d) ÷ (b×c)
content.formula_intro: Fractions are worked out with whole numbers on the top and bottom, then simplified by dividing both by their largest common factor:
content.formula_source: Formula source: standard fraction arithmetic. Only whole numbers are accepted on the top and bottom, and the answer is always simplified. No outside data is used.
example_steps: Start with the fractions: 1/2 + 1/3.
Give them the same bottom number: 1/2 is 3/6 and 1/3 is 2/6.
Add the top numbers: 3 + 2 = 5, so the answer is 5/6.
Answer: 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, which is about 0.83 as a decimal.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 1 over 2, add, 1 over 3, and the result line shows 5/6.
faqs: How do I add fractions with different bottom numbers?
Give them the same bottom number first. For 1/2 + 1/3, use 6: 1/2 is 3/6 and 1/3 is 2/6, so the sum is 5/6. The calculator does this step for you.
How do I divide fractions?
Turn the second fraction upside down and multiply. For 1/2 ÷ 1/4, flip 1/4 to 4/1 and multiply: 1/2 × 4/1 = 4/2 = 2.
Why is the answer simplified?
Because 4/6 and 2/3 are the same amount, and the simplest form is easier to read. The calculator divides the top and bottom by their largest common factor: 4/6 becomes 2/3.
Can the top or bottom number be negative?
Yes. A negative top number makes the fraction negative, and a negative bottom number is moved to the top, so the answer is always shown with the sign on top. For example, 1/−2 is shown as −1/2.
Why can the bottom number not be zero?
Because dividing by zero has no answer in ordinary arithmetic. A fraction with zero on the bottom cannot be worked out, so the calculator shows a clear message instead of a result.
How is the decimal rounded?
The fraction itself is exact and is never rounded. Only the decimal shown under it is rounded, half-up to 2 decimal places: 5/6 is about 0.83. The fraction is the exact answer.

tools.method: No library. Plain JavaScript arithmetic in the browser

content.question: What is the standard deviation of these numbers?
howto: Type at least two numbers in the box, separated by commas. There is no Calculate button — the standard deviation appears as you type.
Read the standard deviation in the result line, rounded half-up to 4 decimal places.
Check the bar and table under the result (Part 5 below) to see the count, the mean and the variance.
content.quick_answer: Standard deviation measures how spread out a set of numbers is around their mean. For example, the numbers 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 have a mean of 5 and a standard deviation of 2.0000. Type your own numbers above, separated by commas, and this calculator gives the mean, the variance and the standard deviation.
content.formula_words: Standard deviation — in words: work out the mean, subtract it from each number, square each difference, average the squares to get the variance, then take the square root.
content.formula_symbol: standard deviation = √(average of (each number − mean)²)
content.formula_intro: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so it is measured in the same units as the numbers themselves:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the population standard deviation, which divides by the count of numbers. It is the version used when your numbers are the whole set, not a sample of a bigger set. No outside data is used.
example_steps: Start with the numbers: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9. There are 8 of them.
Work out the variance: the squared differences from 5 are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4 and 16, which add to 32, and 32 ÷ 8 = 4. The variance is 4.0000.
Answer: the standard deviation is the square root of 4, which is 2.0000.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9, and the result line shows 2.0000.
faqs: What does standard deviation tell me?

How spread out the numbers are around their mean. A small standard deviation means the numbers are close together; a large one means they are spread out. For 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 the mean is 5 and the spread is 2.0000.
What is the difference between population and sample standard deviation?

Population standard deviation divides by the count of numbers, and is used when your numbers are the whole set. Sample standard deviation divides by the count less one, and is used when your numbers are a sample of a bigger set. This page uses the population version, and says so on the page.
What if all the numbers are the same?
The standard deviation is 0.0000, because there is no spread at all. For example, 5, 5, 5, 5 has a mean of 5, a variance of 0 and a standard deviation of 0.
How many numbers do I need?
At least two. With one number there is no spread to measure, so the calculator shows a clear message instead of a result. There is no upper limit except that each number must be under one trillion.
What units is the answer in?
The same units as your numbers. If your numbers are test scores, the standard deviation is in test score points; if they are heights in centimetres, it is in centimetres.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 4 decimal places. For example, the standard deviation of 10, 20 and 30 is 8.1650. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the table, so the figures always agree.

content.question: How much does each person pay, with the tip?

Read what each person pays in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.

content.quick_answer: To split a bill with a tip, work out the tip, add it to the bill, then divide the total by the number of people. For example, a bill of 60 with a 15% tip is 69 in total, so each of 3 people pays 23.00. Type your own figures above and this calculator gives each share instantly.
content.formula_words: Tip and bill split — in words: take the tip percent of the bill, add it to the bill, then divide the total by the number of people.
content.formula_symbol: tip = bill × tip percent ÷ 100; each person pays = (bill + tip) ÷ people
content.formula_intro: The tip is a percent of the bill, and the total is shared out equally:
content.formula_source: Formula source: standard percent arithmetic. The tip percent is typed by you, because tipping customs differ by country and by service. Amounts are in your own currency.
content.example_title: Worked example: bill of 60, 15% tip, 3 people
example_steps: Start with the figures: bill 60, tip 15%, 3 people.
Work out the tip: 60 × 15 ÷ 100 = 9.
Add the tip to the bill: 60 + 9 = 69 in total.
Answer: each of the 3 people pays 69 ÷ 3 = 23.00, of which 3.00 is tip.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 60, 15 and 3, and the result line shows 23.00.
faqs: How much tip should I leave?

It depends on where you are: 15% to 20% is usual in the USA, 10% is common in the UK when service is not already included, and in some countries no tip is expected at all. Type the percent that fits your meal.
Is the tip shared equally too?
Yes, on this page. The tip is added to the bill first, then the total is divided equally, so each person pays the same share of the tip. The table shows the tip per person as well.
What if one person pays for everyone?
Type 1 for the number of people. The share is then the whole total: a bill of 45 with no tip is 45.00 for one person.
What if the bill already includes a service charge?
Then the service charge is already in the bill, so type 0 for the tip percent unless you want to add more. A 0% tip gives each person just their share of the bill.
What if the shares do not divide exactly?

Each share is rounded half-up to 2 decimal places, so the shares can add to a cent more or less than the total. For example, 100 with 20% tip split 3 ways is 40.00 each, which adds to 120.00 exactly; with other numbers a cent can be left over.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. The tip, the total and each share are each rounded on their own, so the shares can differ by a cent from the total. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the table.

content.quick_answer: Sales tax is a percent added to the price before tax. For example, 8% sales tax on a price of 100 is 8, so the total to pay is 108. Type your own price and tax rate above and this calculator gives the sales tax and the total to pay instantly, in your own currency.
content.formula_words: Sales tax — in words: take the tax rate percent of the price, then add that tax to the price.
content.formula_symbol: tax = price × rate ÷ 100, and total = price + tax
content.formula_intro: Sales tax is a percent of the price before tax, added on top at the till:
content.formula_source: Formula source: standard percent arithmetic. The tax rate is typed by you, because sales tax rates differ by state, province and city — this site does not guess your rate. Amounts are in your own currency.

faqs: What is the difference between sales tax and VAT?

Sales tax is added at the till on top of the shelf price, so the price you see is before tax. VAT is usually already included in the shelf price in most countries. This page is for sales tax added on top; the VAT calculator covers tax taken out of a price that already includes it.
What sales tax rate should I type?

Type the combined rate that applies where you buy — state, county and city rates added together where they apply. Rates differ by place and by item, so check the seller or your state tax authority for the rate.
Is sales tax charged on everything?

No. Groceries, medicine and some other items are often exempt or taxed at a lower rate, depending on the state. This calculator does the arithmetic on the price and rate you type; whether the item is taxable is something to check separately.
How do I work out the price before tax from the total?
Divide the total by one plus the rate as a share. If the total is 108 with 8% tax, the price before tax is 108 ÷ 1.08 = 100. The VAT calculator on this site does that sum for you.
Can the tax rate be zero?
Yes. If the item is exempt or the place charges no sales tax, type 0 and the total to pay is exactly the price. The calculator shows that as a real answer.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. For example, 8% tax on 49.99 is 4.00, so the total is 53.99. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the table, so the figures always agree.

content.quick_answer: A loan of $200,000 at 5% a year over 30 years costs $1,073.64 a month. The monthly payment comes from the loan amount, the monthly rate and the number of payments. Each payment first covers that month's interest, and the rest cuts the balance. Over 30 years you pay $386,511.57 in total, of which $186,511.57 is interest.
content.formula_words: Monthly loan payment — in words: the loan amount times the monthly rate, divided by one minus the monthly rate factor for the number of payments.
content.formula_symbol: payment = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), where r is the monthly rate and n is the number of monthly payments
content.formula_intro: A fixed-rate loan is paid off in equal monthly payments. The payment is set so the last payment clears the balance exactly:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard amortisation formula for a fixed-rate loan. No rate is fetched from anywhere — you type your own rate, and the page uses only the three numbers you type.
example_steps: Start with the loan: $200,000, a yearly rate of 5% and a term of 30 years (360 monthly payments).
Turn the yearly rate into a monthly rate: 5% ÷ 12 = 0.4167% a month, or 0.004167 as a decimal.
Answer: the monthly payment is $1,073.64. In month 1, interest is $833.33 and principal is $240.31, so the balance falls to $199,759.69.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 200000, 5 and 30, and the result line shows $1,073.64.
faqs: How is the monthly payment worked out?

The payment comes from the amortisation formula shown on this page: the loan amount, the monthly interest rate and the number of payments. The same payment is due every month for the whole term, so the loan is cleared by the last payment.
Why is most of the first payment interest?

Interest is charged on the balance you still owe, so it is highest at the start when the balance is largest. As the balance falls, the interest part of each payment falls and the principal part grows. That is why the balance falls slowly at first and faster later.
What happens if the interest rate is zero?
With a 0% rate there is no interest at all, so the payment is simply the loan amount divided by the number of months. For example, $120,000 over 10 years at 0% costs $1,000.00 a month.
Does extra payment change the result?

This calculator shows the plan with no extra payments. Paying extra in real life cuts the balance faster, so less interest builds up and the loan ends sooner. Work out the new term by typing a smaller loan amount or a shorter term.
How is the total interest worked out?
Total interest is the monthly payment times the number of payments, minus the loan amount. For $200,000 at 5% over 30 years that is 360 × $1,073.64 − $200,000 = $186,511.57.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is an estimate for planning, worked out from the numbers you type. A real loan also has fees, insurance and terms that change the cost, so check with the lender before you borrow.

content.quick_answer: With rent of $1,500 a month and a $300,000 home bought with a $60,000 deposit at 5% over 10 years, renting is cheaper by $34,604.63. Buying costs the deposit plus the monthly mortgage payment for 10 years, while renting costs the rent for 10 years. The break-even year, when the two totals meet, is about 24 years.
content.formula_words: Rent vs buy — in words: compare the deposit plus the monthly mortgage payment times the months, against the monthly rent times the months.
content.formula_symbol: buying cost = deposit + (monthly payment × months); renting cost = rent × months
content.formula_intro: Both choices are added up over the same number of years. The mortgage payment uses the standard loan formula on a 30-year term:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard amortisation formula for the mortgage payment, plus simple multiplication for the totals. This is a plain cost comparison: it leaves out house price growth, rent rises, tax, upkeep and selling costs, which all change the real answer.
content.example_title: Worked example: rent $1,500 or buy a $300,000 home
example_steps: Start with the numbers: rent $1,500 a month, home price $300,000, deposit $60,000, mortgage rate 5%, 10 years to compare.
The loan is $300,000 − $60,000 = $240,000. On a 30-year term at 5% the monthly payment is $1,288.37.
Buying over 10 years costs $60,000 + 120 × $1,288.37 = $214,604.63. Renting over 10 years costs 120 × $1,500 = $180,000.00.
Answer: renting is cheaper by $34,604.63 over 10 years. The break-even year is about 24 years, when the two totals meet.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 1500, 300000, 60000, 5 and 10, and the result line shows the cheaper choice.
faqs: What does the break-even year mean?

It is the year when the total cost of buying catches up with the total cost of renting. Before that year renting costs less in total; after it, buying costs less in total. It comes from dividing the deposit by the monthly gap between rent and the mortgage payment.
Why does buying look dearer at first?
Buying starts with a large deposit paid on day one, while renting has no deposit. The mortgage payment also stays the same each month, so buying only wins back the deposit slowly, year by year.
Does this count house prices going up?
No. This is a plain cost comparison with no price growth, no rent rises, no tax, no upkeep and no selling costs. If house prices rise fast or rents rise fast, the real answer can be very different.
What mortgage term is used for the payment?

The monthly payment is worked out on a 30-year term at the rate you type. If your real loan has a different term, the payment changes — a shorter term means a higher payment but less interest over time.
Is renting always cheaper for a short stay?
Usually, yes, because the deposit and the buying costs have little time to be won back. For a stay of only a few years, renting is normally cheaper on this plain comparison.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is an estimate for planning, from the numbers you type. Buying a home is a large decision — check the full costs, including tax and upkeep, with a qualified adviser before you act.

content.question: What is the highest home price I can afford from my income and deposit?
howto: Type your yearly income before tax, the deposit you have saved, your other monthly debt payments, the mortgage rate and the mortgage term. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the highest home price in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.
Check the table under the result for the largest monthly payment, the largest loan and the price that follows from them.
content.quick_answer: On an income of $80,000 with a $50,000 deposit, $300 a month of other debts and a 5% mortgage over 30 years, the highest home price is $341,841.20. The rule is that the mortgage payment plus other debts stay under 28% of monthly income. That leaves a largest payment of $1,566.67 a month, supporting a loan of $291,841.20.
content.formula_words: House affordability — in words: take 28% of monthly income, subtract other monthly debts, then work out the largest loan that payment supports and add the deposit.
content.formula_symbol: largest payment = (yearly income ÷ 12 × 28%) − monthly debts; largest price = largest loan + deposit
content.formula_intro: Lenders often use the 28% rule: housing costs should stay under 28% of gross monthly income. The largest loan is found by running the loan formula backwards:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the common 28% housing-cost rule, with the standard amortisation formula run backwards to find the loan. This is a planning guide only — a lender uses your credit history, job, debts and deposit, and may lend more or less than this figure.
example_steps: Start with the numbers: yearly income $80,000, deposit $50,000, other debts $300 a month, rate 5%, term 30 years.
Monthly income is $80,000 ÷ 12 = $6,666.67. 28% of that is $1,866.67, minus $300 of debts leaves a largest payment of $1,566.67 a month.
At 5% over 30 years, a payment of $1,566.67 supports a loan of $291,841.20.
Answer: the highest home price is $291,841.20 + $50,000 = $341,841.20.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 80000, 50000, 300, 5 and 30, and the result line shows $341,841.20.
faqs: Why 28% of income?

28% is the common housing-cost rule lenders have used for years: the mortgage payment should stay under 28% of gross monthly income. It is a guide, not a law — some lenders allow more, and some buyers are safer with less.
Do my other debts matter?

Yes. Other monthly debts — car loans, cards, student loans — are taken off the 28% amount first, because that money is already spoken for. Higher debts mean a smaller largest payment and a lower home price.
What if my debts are higher than 28% of my income?
Then the largest payment is zero or less, and this calculator shows that no loan fits the 28% rule. Paying down debts or raising the deposit are the two ways to change that answer.
Does a bigger deposit raise the price I can afford?
Yes, dollar for dollar: the highest price is the largest loan plus the deposit. A $20,000 larger deposit raises the highest price by $20,000, and it also cuts the loan you need.
Does the mortgage term change the answer?
Yes. A longer term spreads the loan over more payments, so the same monthly payment supports a larger loan — but you pay much more interest over the whole term.
Is this a promise that a lender will lend this much?
No. This is an estimate for planning only. A lender checks your credit history, job, debts and deposit, and may lend more or less. Talk to a lender or a qualified adviser before you act.

Read the deposit amount in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.
Check the table under the result for the deposit, the loan left to borrow and the same figures at 5%, 10% and 20%.
content.quick_answer: A 20% deposit on a $300,000 home is $60,000, which leaves a loan of $240,000 to borrow. The deposit is the home price times the deposit percent divided by 100. A larger deposit means a smaller loan, a smaller monthly payment and less interest over the life of the loan.
content.formula_words: Down payment — in words: multiply the home price by the deposit percent, then divide by 100.
content.formula_symbol: deposit = home price × deposit percent ÷ 100; loan = home price − deposit
content.formula_intro: The deposit is a percent of the price. The rest is the loan you need to borrow:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard arithmetic definition of percent. No rate is fetched from anywhere — you type the price and the percent, and the page uses only those two numbers.
content.example_title: Worked example: 20% deposit on a $300,000 home
example_steps: Start with the numbers: home price $300,000, deposit percent 20%.
Turn the percent into a share: 20 ÷ 100 = 0.20.
Multiply the price by the share: $300,000 × 0.20 = $60,000.
Answer: the deposit is $60,000.00, and the loan left to borrow is $300,000 − $60,000 = $240,000.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 300000 and 20, and the result line shows $60,000.00.
faqs: How much deposit do I need?

It depends on the lender and the loan. 20% is the common target because it often avoids extra insurance, but many loans allow 10%, 5% or even less. A smaller deposit means a larger loan and a higher monthly payment.
What is the loan after the deposit?
The loan is the home price minus the deposit. On a $300,000 home with a $60,000 deposit, the loan is $240,000. This calculator shows that figure in the table under your result.
Does a bigger deposit save money?

Yes. A bigger deposit means a smaller loan, so the monthly payment is smaller and the total interest over the loan is smaller. It also leaves you owing less than the home is worth, which lenders like.
Can the deposit percent be over 100?
No sensible deposit is over 100% of the price — that would be more than the home costs. If you type a percent over 100, the calculator shows a clear message instead of a made-up number.
What if the deposit percent is zero?
A 0% deposit means a deposit of $0.00 and a loan for the full price. Some loans allow that, but the monthly payment is at its highest and the lender may add extra costs.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is an estimate for planning, from the numbers you type. Deposit rules change by lender and by country, so check with the lender before you act.

content.question: Does refinancing my mortgage save money, and when do the fees pay for themselves?
howto: Type the loan balance left, your current rate, the new rate, the new loan term and the refinancing fees. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the monthly saving in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.
Check the table under the result for both monthly payments, the break-even month and the saving over the full term.
content.quick_answer: Refinancing a $200,000 balance from 7% to 5% over 30 years saves $256.96 a month. The old payment is $1,330.60 and the new payment is $1,073.64. The $4,000 fees pay for themselves in 16 months, because $4,000 divided by $256.96 is 15.6 months, rounded up. After that month, the saving is yours to keep.
content.formula_words: Refinance saving — in words: work out the monthly payment at the old rate and at the new rate, then subtract; divide the fees by the monthly saving for the break-even month.
content.formula_symbol: monthly saving = old payment − new payment; break-even months = fees ÷ monthly saving, rounded up
content.formula_intro: Each payment uses the standard loan formula on the same balance and term, once at the old rate and once at the new rate:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard amortisation formula for a fixed-rate loan. No rate is fetched from anywhere — you type both rates, and the page uses only the five numbers you type.
example_steps: Start with the numbers: balance $200,000, current rate 7%, new rate 5%, term 30 years, fees $4,000.
The old payment at 7% over 30 years is $1,330.60 a month. The new payment at 5% is $1,073.64 a month.
Answer: you save $256.96 a month, and the fees pay for themselves in 16 months ($4,000 ÷ $256.96 = 15.6, rounded up).
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 200000, 7, 5, 30 and 4000, and the result line shows the monthly saving.
faqs: What is the break-even month?

It is the month when the savings so far have covered the refinancing fees. With $4,000 of fees and $256.96 saved a month, that is month 16. Before that month you are still out of pocket; after it, every month saves you money.
What if the new rate is higher than the old rate?
Then refinancing costs more each month, and there is no break-even month — the fees never pay for themselves. The calculator says so plainly instead of showing a saving that does not exist.
Does a shorter new term change the answer?

Yes. A shorter term means a higher monthly payment, so the monthly saving shrinks or turns into an extra cost — but the loan ends years sooner and the total interest falls a lot. Compare the total saving over the term in the table, not just the monthly figure.
Are the fees added to the loan?

In this calculator the fees are paid on their own and counted in the break-even month. In real life some lenders add the fees to the loan balance, which raises the new payment and pushes the break-even month later.
Should I refinance for a small saving?
Only if you will stay in the home past the break-even month. If you move or refinance again before then, the fees cost more than you saved.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is an estimate for planning, from the numbers you type. Refinancing has tax and legal effects that differ by country, so check with a qualified adviser before you act.

faqs: Should I compare the monthly payment or the total interest?
Compare the total interest when the loan amounts are the same — it is the true cost of borrowing. A loan can have a lower monthly payment but cost more in total if it runs for longer.
Can a loan with a higher rate still be cheaper?

Yes, if its term is much shorter. Interest builds up month by month, so a short loan at a higher rate can cost less in total than a long loan at a lower rate. This calculator shows both figures so you can see it.
What if the two loans are for different amounts?

Then compare the total paid for each loan, and think about what you get for the extra money. The verdict here is on total interest, which is fair only when the amounts match — the table shows the monthly payment and total paid for each loan too.
Do fees change the answer?

Yes. Fees are not in this comparison — only the loan amount, rate and term. A loan with a low rate but high fees can cost more in real life, so add the fees to the loan amount before you compare, or count them on their own.
What does total interest leave out?
It leaves out fees, insurance and any late-payment charges. It is the interest alone, worked out from the rate and term you type.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is an estimate for planning, from the numbers you type. Check the full terms with each lender before you borrow.

content.question: How long will it take to clear my credit card balance at this monthly payment?

content.quick_answer: A $5,000 card balance at 20% a year, paid off at $200 a month, takes 33 months to clear and costs $1,522.10 in interest. Each month interest is added to the balance first, then your payment cuts it down. The last payment is smaller than $200, because only a small balance is left by then.
content.formula_words: Credit card payoff — in words: each month add one month of interest to the balance, then take off the payment, and repeat until the balance reaches zero.
content.formula_symbol: months = −ln(1 − balance × monthly rate ÷ payment) ÷ ln(1 + monthly rate); the table counts month by month for the exact interest
content.formula_intro: The payoff time comes from the same sum the table counts month by month: interest is added, then the payment is taken off, until nothing is left:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard loan payoff formula, checked month by month in the table on this page. No rate is fetched from anywhere — you type your own rate, and the page uses only the three numbers you type.
content.example_title: Worked example: $5,000 at 20%, paying $200 a month
example_steps: Start with the numbers: balance $5,000, yearly rate 20% (1.6667% a month), payment $200 a month.
In month 1, interest is $5,000 × 1.6667% = $83.33. After the $200 payment the balance is $5,000 + $83.33 − $200 = $4,883.33.
The same step repeats each month. The balance falls faster as the interest shrinks, and the last payment is smaller than $200.
Answer: the card is clear in 33 months, and the total interest paid is $1,522.10.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 5000, 20 and 200, and the result line shows 33 months.
faqs: Why does it take longer than the balance divided by the payment?
Because interest is added every month. $5,000 divided by $200 is 25 months, but the interest adds $1,522.10 along the way, so the real time is 33 months. Only a 0% rate would give 25 months.
What if my payment does not cover the monthly interest?

Then the balance never falls — it grows. For example, a $50 payment on a $5,000 balance at 20% cannot cover the $83.33 of interest in the first month. The calculator says so plainly instead of showing a payoff time that does not exist.
Does paying more each month help a lot?

Yes, more than most people expect. A higher payment cuts the balance faster, so less interest builds up, and the card is clear much sooner. Try a larger payment in the tool above and watch the months and the interest fall.
Why is the last payment smaller?
Because the balance left in the last month is smaller than the usual payment. You only pay what is left, plus that month's interest — never a full $200 for a balance of $20.
Does this count new spending on the card?
No. This counts the balance you type, with no new spending added. Any new spending adds to the balance and pushes the payoff date later.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is an estimate for planning, from the numbers you type. Card rates and fees change, so check your own card statement before you act.
