content.quick_answer: With $1,000 a month to pay three debts of $3,000 at 20%, $5,000 at 10% and $2,000 at 15%, snowball clears them in 11 months with $614.09 of interest, while avalanche also takes 11 months but costs $584.66 of interest. Snowball pays the smallest debt first; avalanche pays the highest rate first.
content.formula_words: Debt payoff — in words: each month add one month of interest to every debt, then pay the debts in the chosen order until the monthly payment is used up, and repeat until all debts reach zero.
content.formula_symbol: each month: balance grows by balance × yearly rate ÷ 12, then the payment is used up in order — smallest balance first (snowball) or highest rate first (avalanche)
content.formula_intro: Both methods use the same monthly count. Only the order changes. The count runs month by month until every balance reaches zero:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard month-by-month loan payoff count, run twice — once in snowball order and once in avalanche order. No rate is fetched from anywhere — you type your own rates, and the page uses only the numbers you type. The count leaves out minimum payments and fees.
content.example_title: Worked example: three debts, $1,000 a month
example_steps: Start with the numbers: $1,000 a month to pay debts of $3,000 at 20%, $5,000 at 10% and $2,000 at 15%.

Snowball order is smallest first: the $2,000 debt, then the $3,000 debt, then the $5,000 debt. Avalanche order is highest rate first: the $3,000 debt at 20%, then the $2,000 debt at 15%, then the $5,000 debt at 10%.
Each month, interest is added to every debt, then the $1,000 payment is used up in order, clearing one debt before moving to the next.
Answer: both orders take 11 months, but snowball costs $614.09 in interest and avalanche costs $584.66 — avalanche saves $29.43 here.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 1000, then 3000 at 20, 5000 at 10 and 2000 at 15, and the result line shows both orders.
faqs: What is the snowball method?

Snowball pays the smallest debt first, whatever its rate. Clearing a whole debt quickly feels like a win and frees up money for the next debt. It can cost more interest than avalanche, but many people stick with it longer.
What is the avalanche method?

Avalanche pays the highest-rate debt first, whatever its size. That cuts the most interest, so it is usually the cheapest way to clear all the debts. In the example above it saves $29.43 against snowball.
Which method should I choose?

Avalanche costs less interest in almost every case. Snowball wins only if quick wins keep you going when a big high-rate debt would feel endless. Pick the one you will actually stick with — a plan you drop costs more than either method.
How do I use this for more than three debts?
Add the smallest debts together, or run the calculator twice: first for the three debts you will clear first, then again for the rest with the payment you will have after those are gone.
What if my payment does not cover the interest?

Then the debts never fall — they grow. The calculator says so plainly instead of showing a payoff date that does not exist. Raise the payment above the first month's interest, or the count has no end.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is an estimate for planning, from the numbers you type. It leaves out minimum payments, fees and rate changes, so check your own statements before you act.

content.question: How should I split my monthly income into needs, wants and savings?
howto: Type your monthly income after tax in the box. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the three amounts in the result line: needs, wants and savings.
Check the bar and table under the result to see the 50%, 30% and 20% split drawn from your income.
content.quick_answer: On a monthly income of $4,000 after tax, the 50/30/20 budget gives $2,000.00 for needs, $1,200.00 for wants and $800.00 for savings. Needs are the bills you must pay, like rent and food. Wants are the extras you enjoy, like eating out. Savings cover debt payoff and money put aside for later.
content.formula_words: 50/30/20 budget — in words: half of your income after tax goes to needs, three tenths to wants, and two tenths to savings.
content.formula_symbol: needs = income × 50 ÷ 100; wants = income × 30 ÷ 100; savings = income × 20 ÷ 100
content.formula_intro: The 50/30/20 rule splits income after tax into three parts that always add up to the whole income:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the 50/30/20 budgeting rule, a common planning guide. No data is fetched from anywhere — you type your own income, and the page uses only that one number.
content.example_title: Worked example: $4,000 a month after tax
example_steps: Start with the number: monthly income after tax is $4,000.
Answer: needs $2,000.00, wants $1,200.00 and savings $800.00 — and $2,000 + $1,200 + $800 = $4,000, the whole income.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 4000, and the result line shows the three amounts.
faqs: What counts as a need?
A need is a bill you must pay to live and work: rent or mortgage, food, power, water, transport to work, insurance and minimum debt payments. If you stopped paying it, life would break down quickly.
What counts as a want?

A want is spending you enjoy but could live without: eating out, films, holidays, new clothes you do not need, and streaming services. Wants are not bad — they are planned, at 30%, instead of taking money from savings.
What counts as savings?
Savings are money put aside for later: an emergency fund, extra debt payoff above the minimum, and money for retirement or a deposit. Paying off a costly debt counts here, because it saves interest.
What if my needs cost more than 50%?
That is common where rent is high. Cut wants first, then look for a cheaper need — a smaller home, a cheaper phone plan — and raise income if you can. The 50% figure is a target, not a pass mark.
Should the split use income before or after tax?
After tax, because that is the money that actually reaches you. Using income before tax would plan spending with money you never see.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is a planning guide, from the number you type. A budget that fits your real bills matters more than hitting 50/30/20 exactly.

content.question: What is money from a past year worth today after inflation?
howto: Type the amount from the past year, how many years ago it was, and the yearly inflation rate you assume. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the amount in today's money in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.
Check the table under the result for the rise in dollars, the rise in percent and the same amount at 2% and 5%.
content.quick_answer: An amount of $100 from 10 years ago is worth $134.39 in today's money at a yearly inflation rate of 3% that you enter yourself. Prices rise a little each year, so the same basket of goods costs more now. This site does not fetch any live inflation rate — the rate you type is your own assumption.
content.formula_words: Inflation — in words: take the past amount and grow it by the yearly inflation rate, once for each year, compounding year after year.
content.formula_symbol: today's amount = past amount × (1 + yearly rate ÷ 100)^years
content.formula_intro: Inflation compounds, like interest in reverse: each year's rise builds on the last year's higher price:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard compound growth formula. The inflation rate is an assumption you type — this site holds no inflation data and fetches no live rate. For a real figure, use the official inflation rate for the country and years you mean.
content.example_title: Worked example: $100 from 10 years ago at 3% a year
example_steps: Start with the numbers: amount $100, years 10, yearly inflation rate 3% (your own assumption).
The yearly factor is 1 + 3 ÷ 100 = 1.03.
Raise it to 10 years: 1.03^10 = 1.3439, then multiply: $100 × 1.3439 = $134.39.
Answer: $100 from 10 years ago buys what $134.39 buys today — a rise of $34.39, or 34.39%.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 100, 10 and 3, and the result line shows $134.39.
faqs: Where does the inflation rate come from?

From you. This site does not fetch any live inflation rate, so you type the yearly rate you want to assume. For a real check, look up the official inflation rate for your country and years — for example the national statistics office.
Why does inflation compound?

Because each year's price rise applies to the new, higher price, not to the old one. At 3% a year, prices rise 3% in year one, then 3% of the higher price in year two, and so on. That is why 10 years at 3% gives 34.39%, not 30%.
What is the difference between inflation and the cost of living?
Inflation is the general rise in prices over time. The cost of living is what you actually pay, which depends on what you buy. Your own costs can rise faster or slower than the general rate.
Can the inflation rate be zero or negative?
Yes. A 0% rate means prices stay the same, so $100 stays $100. A negative rate means prices fall, so the amount in today's money is smaller than the past amount.
How many years can I count?
This calculator counts up to 100 years. Beyond that the numbers stop meaning much, because no rate stays steady for that long.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is an estimate for planning, from the numbers you type, with a rate you assume. It is not a forecast of real prices.

faqs: Does this site fetch live exchange rates?
No. This site never fetches a live rate. You type the rate yourself, and the page says so on the page. Check a current rate from your bank or a rate source, then type it in.
What rate should I type?
The rate for the two currencies and the day you mean, from your bank or a rate source. Rates move during the day, so a rate from last week can give a different answer from today's rate.
Why did my bank give me less than this answer?
Banks and cards often add a fee or use a worse rate than the headline rate. This calculator shows the plain sum with no fee, so the amount you receive can be less.
What is the reverse rate?
It is 1 divided by the rate you typed. At a rate of 1.27, the reverse rate is 0.7874 — one unit of the second currency is worth 0.7874 units of the first. The table under your result shows it.
Can the rate be less than 1?
Yes. A rate under 1 means one unit of the first currency is worth less than one unit of the second. For example, 250 at a rate of 0.85 converts to 212.50.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is a plain multiplication for planning, from the numbers you type. It is not a quote, and it is not a promise of what you will receive.

content.quick_answer: A man of 180 cm with a 90 cm waist and a 40 cm neck has about 18.4% body fat by the US Navy method. It uses height, waist and neck for men, and adds the hip for women. It is a guide only, from the numbers you type — not medical advice, and never a replacement for a doctor.
content.formula_words: Body fat (US Navy method) — in words: the result comes from the logs of the waist, neck and height measurements for men, with the hip added for women.
content.formula_intro: The US Navy method estimates body fat from tape measurements instead of a scan. All measurements are in centimetres:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the US Navy body fat formula, the version used by the US Department of Defense. It is an estimate, not a scan, and it can be off by a few percent for very muscular or very lean people.
content.example_title: Worked example: man, 180 cm, waist 90 cm, neck 40 cm
example_steps: Start with the numbers: male, height 180 cm, waist 90 cm, neck 40 cm.
Waist minus neck is 90 − 40 = 50 cm. The log of 50 is 1.6990 and the log of 180 is 2.2553.

content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: choose male and type 30, 180, 90, 40 and 0, and the result line shows 18.4%.
faqs: How exact is the US Navy method?

It is an estimate, usually within a few percent of a scan. It works best for average builds. Very muscular people can read higher than they are, because muscle makes the neck and waist thicker, and very lean people can read lower.
Why do women need a hip measurement?
Because women carry more fat around the hips, so the hip size carries real information about body fat. For men the waist and neck are enough, so the hip box is left at 0.
How should I measure my waist?
Stand relaxed and measure around the waist at the navel, with the tape level and snug but not tight. Do not breathe in. Measure twice and use the average if the two readings differ.
What is a healthy body fat percent?

For men, roughly 10–20% is the fitness range and 21–24% is average; for women, roughly 16–24% is the fitness range and 25–31% is average. These are guides, not medical limits, and age and sport change them.
Why does the calculator stop when the waist is smaller than the neck?
Because the formula takes the log of waist minus neck, and the log of zero or a negative number has no answer. A waist smaller than the neck is a measuring mistake — check the tape and try again.
Is this medical advice?
No. This is a general guide only, worked out from the numbers you type. It is not a diagnosis and never replaces advice from a doctor or another health professional.

faqs: What is a healthy body mass index?

The World Health Organization calls 18.5 to 24.9 healthy for most adults. Under 18.5 is underweight, 25 to 29.9 is overweight, and 30 or more is obese. These are ranges for groups, not a verdict on one person.
What is the Devine ideal weight?

It is an older formula from medicine: 50 kg for a man or 45.5 kg for a woman at 5 feet tall, plus 2.3 kg for each inch above 5 feet. It gives one number, while the index range gives a range — both are guides.
Why is it a range, not one number?
Because healthy weight depends on build, muscle and age. Two people of the same height can both be healthy at different weights. A range is more honest than one number.
Does muscle change the answer?
Yes. Muscle weighs more than fat, so a muscular person can sit above the range and still be healthy, while a person with little muscle can sit inside the range and still carry too much fat.
Can I type my height in inches?
This page takes centimetres. To change inches to centimetres, multiply the inches by 2.54 — for example, 69 inches is 175 cm.
Is this medical advice?
No. This is a general guide only, worked out from the number you type. It is not a diagnosis and never replaces advice from a doctor or another health professional.

Protein and carbs give 4 calories per gram, fat gives 9. The three percents must add up to 100, or the calculator shows a clear message instead of a made-up answer.
content.formula_words: Macros — in words: take the calories for each macro, divide protein and carbs by 4 and fat by 9, to get grams.
content.formula_symbol: protein grams = calories × protein% ÷ 100 ÷ 4; carb grams = calories × carb% ÷ 100 ÷ 4; fat grams = calories × fat% ÷ 100 ÷ 9
content.formula_intro: Each gram of protein or carbs gives 4 calories, and each gram of fat gives 9 calories. Working backwards from calories gives grams:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard energy values of 4 calories per gram for protein and carbs and 9 calories per gram for fat. No data is fetched from anywhere — you type your own calories and split, and the page uses only those four numbers.
example_steps: Start with the numbers: 2,000 calories a day, split 30% protein, 40% carbs, 30% fat.

faqs: Why must the percents add up to 100?

Because the three macros together make up all of your calories. If they add up to 90 or 110, some calories are missing or counted twice, so no honest answer exists. The calculator shows a clear message until the split adds up to 100.
Why does fat give fewer grams than protein for the same calories?
Because fat is more energy-dense: 9 calories per gram against 4 for protein and carbs. The same 600 calories is 150 g of protein but only 67 g of fat.
What split should I use?

A common starting split is 30% protein, 40% carbs and 30% fat. People who train hard often raise protein, and people who eat low-carb raise fat. Your own goal and your doctor's advice matter more than any one split.
Where do my daily calories come from?
From your total daily energy use — your base rate plus activity. Use the calorie tool on this site to work that out first, then type the number here.
Are the grams rounded?
Yes, to whole numbers, half-up. For example, 66.67 g of fat rounds to 67 g. The calories in the table use the same rounded grams, so the figures agree.
Is this medical or diet advice?
No. This is a general guide only, worked out from the numbers you type. It is not a diet plan and never replaces advice from a doctor or a dietitian.

content.question: What is my running pace per kilometre and per mile?
howto: Type the distance you ran in kilometres and the time it took in minutes. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.

content.quick_answer: Running 10 km in 50 minutes is a pace of 5:00 min/km, which is 8:03 min/mile. The pace per kilometre is the time divided by the distance, and the pace per mile is the same time over the distance in miles. Your speed is 12.00 km/h, or 7.46 miles per hour.
content.formula_words: Running pace — in words: divide the time in minutes by the distance, for the pace per kilometre; multiply by 1.60934 for the pace per mile.
content.formula_symbol: pace per km = time in minutes ÷ distance in km; pace per mile = pace per km × 1.60934; speed = distance ÷ time in hours
content.formula_intro: Pace is time per unit of distance. One mile is 1.60934 kilometres, so the mile pace is always the kilometre pace times 1.60934:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard definitions of pace and speed, with 1 mile = 1.60934 km. No data is fetched from anywhere — you type your own distance and time, and the page uses only those two numbers.
example_steps: Start with the numbers: distance 10 km, time 50 minutes.
Pace per kilometre: 50 ÷ 10 = 5.00 minutes, which is 5:00 min/km.
Pace per mile: 5.00 × 1.60934 = 8.05 minutes, which is 8:03 min/mile (0.05 minutes is 3 seconds).
Answer: 5:00 min/km, 8:03 min/mile. Speed is 10 km ÷ (50 ÷ 60) hours = 12.00 km/h.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 10 and 50, and the result line shows 5:00 min/km, 8:03 min/mile.
faqs: How do I type a time with seconds?
Type the time as minutes with a decimal: 50 minutes 30 seconds is 50.5 minutes. The pace is shown in minutes and seconds, rounded to the nearest second.
Why is the mile pace slower than the kilometre pace?
Because a mile is longer than a kilometre — 1.60934 km. It takes longer to cover a mile than a kilometre at the same speed, so the minutes per mile are always higher.
What is a good pace?
It depends on the distance and on you. A 5:00 min/km pace over 10 km is strong for a regular runner; over a marathon it is very fast. Compare your pace with your own past runs, not with strangers.
Can I use miles for the distance?
This page takes kilometres. To change miles to kilometres, multiply the miles by 1.60934 — for example, 6.2 miles is 10 km.
What if the distance is zero?
A pace over zero distance has no answer, because the sum divides by the distance. The calculator shows a clear message instead of a made-up number.
Is this medical advice?
No. This is a plain time-and-distance sum. Build up distance slowly, and ask a doctor before starting hard training if you have a health condition.

content.quick_answer: If the first day of your last period was 3 August 2026, the estimated due date is 10 May 2027. The date is the first day of the last period plus 280 days, which is 40 weeks. This is an estimate only, not medical advice, and only a scan can date a pregnancy exactly.
content.formula_words: Due date — in words: add 280 days, which is 40 weeks, to the first day of the last period.
content.formula_symbol: due date = first day of last period + 280 days
content.formula_intro: Pregnancy is counted as 40 weeks from the first day of the last period, even though conception happens about two weeks later. The rule is called Naegele's rule:
content.formula_source: Formula source: Naegele's rule, the standard 280-day count used in pregnancy care. This is an estimate only, not medical advice — only a scan and a doctor can date a pregnancy exactly, and few babies arrive on the exact due date.
content.example_title: Worked example: last period started 3 August 2026
example_steps: Start with the date: the first day of the last period was 3 August 2026.
Add 40 weeks, which is 280 days, to that date.

content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: pick 3 August 2026, and the result line shows 10 May 2027.
faqs: Why 280 days?

Pregnancy is counted as 40 weeks from the first day of the last period. Conception usually happens about two weeks after that date, so the baby is really about 38 weeks old at the due date — but the 40-week count is the standard doctors use.
How exact is the due date?
It is an estimate. Only about 1 in 20 babies arrive on the exact due date, and most arrive within two weeks either side. A scan in early pregnancy dates the pregnancy more exactly than this count.
What if I do not know the first day of my last period?
Then this calculator cannot give a date — the whole sum starts from that day. Ask your doctor, who can date the pregnancy from a scan instead.
What does the week of pregnancy mean?

It is the number of full weeks from the first day of the last period to today. The table under your result shows it, with the trimester: weeks 1–13 are the first, 14–27 the second, and 28–40 the third.
What if the date I pick is in the future?
A last period cannot start in the future, so the calculator shows a clear message instead of a due date. Pick a date in the past.
Is this medical advice?
No. This is an estimate only, not medical advice. It never replaces care from a doctor or a midwife — talk to them about your pregnancy, your due date and any worries.

content.question: What is my GPA from my course grades and credit hours?
howto: Choose a grade from A to F and type the credit hours for each course you took. Leave a course on No course if you did not take it. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the GPA in the result line, on the 4.0 scale, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.
Check the table under the result for the total grade points, the total credits and each course's share.
content.quick_answer: With A in a 3-credit course, B in a 3-credit course and A in a 4-credit course, the GPA is 3.70. Each grade is worth points — A is 4, B is 3, C is 2, D is 1 and F is 0 — and the GPA is total grade points divided by total credits. More credits means more weight.
content.formula_words: GPA — in words: turn each grade into points, multiply by the course credits, add them up, and divide by the total credits.
content.formula_symbol: GPA = (grade points × credits, added over all courses) ÷ total credits; A = 4, B = 3, C = 2, D = 1, F = 0
content.formula_intro: GPA is a weighted average on the 4.0 scale. The weight is the credit hours, so a 4-credit course counts more than a 3-credit course:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard 4.0 GPA scale used by schools and colleges in the USA and Canada. No data is fetched from anywhere — you type your own grades and credits, and the page uses only those numbers.
content.example_title: Worked example: A (3 credits), B (3 credits), A (4 credits)
example_steps: Start with the courses: A in 3 credits, B in 3 credits, A in 4 credits.
Turn grades into points: A is 4, B is 3. Course points are 4 × 3 = 12, 3 × 3 = 9, and 4 × 4 = 16.
Add the points: 12 + 9 + 16 = 37. Add the credits: 3 + 3 + 4 = 10.
Answer: GPA = 37 ÷ 10 = 3.70.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: choose A, B and A with 3, 3 and 4 credits, and the result line shows 3.70.
faqs: What do the letters mean in points?
On the 4.0 scale, A is worth 4 points, B is 3, C is 2, D is 1 and F is 0. Some schools add plus and minus grades, like A− at 3.7 — this calculator uses the plain letters only.
Why do credits matter?
Because the GPA is weighted by credits. An A in a 4-credit course pulls the GPA up more than an A in a 1-credit course, and an F in a 4-credit course pulls it down more.
What is a good GPA?
On the 4.0 scale, 3.5 and above is usually strong, 3.0 is a solid B average, and below 2.0 can put you on probation at many schools. What counts as good depends on your school and your goal.
What if I have more than four courses?

Work out the GPA for four courses at a time, then combine the results: add all the grade points together and divide by all the credits together. Or run the calculator again with the other courses and combine the two totals by hand.
Does a failed course count?
Yes. An F is worth 0 points but its credits still count in the total, so it pulls the GPA down. Leaving the course out would give a wrong, higher GPA.
Is this an official GPA?
No. This is a plain weighted average from the grades and credits you type. Your school may count plus and minus grades, repeated courses or transfer credits differently — check its own rules.

content.question: How do I convert this value between units — length, weight, volume, temperature, area or speed?
howto: Type the value, choose what you are converting — length, weight, volume, temperature, area or speed — then choose the from unit and the to unit. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the converted value in the result line, rounded half-up to 4 decimal places.
Check the table under the result for the reverse conversion and the same value in the other units of that kind.
content.quick_answer: 10 metres converts to 32.8084 feet, because 1 metre is 3.28084 feet. This page converts length, weight, volume, temperature, area and speed between metric and imperial units, using fixed conversion factors. No live data is used — the factors never change, so the answer is the same today as it was last year.
content.formula_words: Unit conversion — in words: change the value into the base unit of its kind, then change it out of the base unit into the unit you want. Temperature uses its own formula instead.
content.formula_symbol: converted value = value × (from unit in base units) ÷ (to unit in base units); temperature: °F = °C × 9 ÷ 5 + 32
content.formula_intro: Every unit in a kind is a fixed multiple of one base unit — metres for length, kilograms for weight, litres for volume. The sum goes through the base unit:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard fixed conversion factors — 1 mile = 1.60934 km, 1 kg = 2.20462 lb, 1 US gallon = 3.78541 litres, and the same for the rest. Temperature uses the standard Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin formulas. No live data is used.
example_steps: Start with the numbers: value 10, kind length, from metres, to feet.
The factor is 1 metre = 3.28084 feet.
Answer: 10 metres is 32.8084 feet. Back the other way, 32.8084 feet ÷ 3.28084 = 10 metres.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 10, choose length, metres and feet, and the result line shows 32.8084 ft.
faqs: Why is the answer given to 4 decimal places?

Because conversions often need more precision than money does. 10 metres is 32.8084 feet, not 32.81 — the extra places keep the answer exact enough to work with, and the same 4-place rule is used everywhere on this page.
Which gallon does this use?
The US gallon of 3.78541 litres, which is the gallon used on most recipes and fuel figures in the USA. The UK imperial gallon is larger, at 4.54609 litres, and is not on this page.
Why is temperature different from the rest?

Because temperature scales do not start at the same zero. Length and weight are simple multiples, but Celsius and Fahrenheit are shifted as well as scaled, so the sum needs its own formula — and Kelvin starts at absolute zero.
Can I convert between kinds, like metres to kilograms?
No. A length cannot become a weight — the units measure different things. The calculator only converts inside one kind, and the from and to boxes always show units of the kind you chose.
What if the from and to units are the same?
Then the answer is the value itself — 10 metres is 10 metres. That is a real answer, not an error.
Is anything fetched from the internet for this?
No. The conversion factors are fixed numbers written into the page, and the whole sum runs in your browser. Nothing you type is sent anywhere.

content.question: What is the final price after discount, tax and tip are all applied?
howto: Type the price, the discount percent, the tax percent and the tip percent. Put 0 for any step that does not apply. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the final amount to pay in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.

content.quick_answer: A $100 bill with a 10% discount, 8% tax and a 15% tip comes to $111.78 in total. The discount comes off first, leaving $90.00, then tax of $7.20 takes it to $97.20, then a tip of $14.58 on that total gives $111.78. The order matters, because tax and tip are worked out on the discounted price.
content.formula_words: Tip, tax and discount — in words: take the discount off the price, add tax on what is left, then add the tip on the taxed total.
content.formula_symbol: discounted price = price × (1 − discount% ÷ 100); tax = discounted price × tax% ÷ 100; tip = (discounted price + tax) × tip% ÷ 100; total = discounted price + tax + tip
content.formula_intro: The three steps run in a fixed order — discount first, then tax, then tip — because tax and tip are worked out on the price after discount:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard arithmetic of percent off, percent tax and percent tip, in the order discount, tax, tip. No rate is fetched from anywhere — you type your own percents, and the page uses only the four numbers you type.
content.example_title: Worked example: $100 with 10% off, 8% tax, 15% tip
example_steps: Start with the numbers: price $100, discount 10%, tax 8%, tip 15%.
Discount first: $100 × (1 − 10 ÷ 100) = $90.00. The saving is $10.00.
Tax on the discounted price: $90.00 × 8 ÷ 100 = $7.20, so the total is $97.20. Tip on that total: $97.20 × 15 ÷ 100 = $14.58.
Answer: the final amount is $97.20 + $14.58 = $111.78.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 100, 10, 8 and 15, and the result line shows $111.78.
faqs: Why does the order matter?

Because tax and tip are worked out on the price after discount. If the tip were worked out on the full $100 instead of $97.20, it would be $15.00 instead of $14.58, and the total would be $112.20 — a different answer.
Should the tip be on the price before or after tax?
This calculator puts the tip on the price after tax, which is how many people tip in the USA. Some people tip on the price before tax instead — that gives a smaller tip, and a smaller total.
What if there is no discount, tax or tip?
Put 0 for that step and it is skipped. With 0% discount, 0% tax and 0% tip, the total is just the price you typed.
Can the discount be more than 100%?
No sensible discount is over 100% — that would make the price negative. If you type a discount over 100, the calculator shows a clear message instead of a made-up number.
Does this split the bill between people?
No. This gives the final total for one bill. To split it, use the tip and bill split tool on this site, which divides a total between people.
Is this financial advice?
No. This is a plain percent sum for planning, from the numbers you type. Tax rules differ by place, so check the rate where you are.

faqs: Should I compare salary alone, or the whole offer?

Compare the whole offer. A job with a lower salary can still be worth more once the bonus, pension, health cover and paid time off are added in. This calculator adds salary, bonus and benefits for each offer so the totals can be compared fairly.
How do I put a value on benefits?

Use the yearly cash value: what the benefit would cost you to buy yourself, or what the employer states it is worth. For a pension, use the yearly employer contribution. If a benefit has no clear cash value, leave it out of both offers and weigh it separately.
Does this calculator take tax off the offers?

No. It compares the totals before tax, because tax depends on your full income, your country and your tax code. If the two offers are in different countries, compare them with the Salary Country Comparison Calculator as well.
What if the offers have different working hours?

Then divide each total by its yearly working hours to get the pay per hour. An offer worth $70,000 for a 35-hour week pays more per hour than $72,000 for a 45-hour week. Hours are not part of this page, so work that step out by hand.
What if one offer has a signing bonus?

Add a one-off signing bonus to that offer only in the first year, and say so when you compare. This page treats every amount as yearly, so a one-off bonus added here would overstate the offer in later years.
Is this calculator free, and do I need to sign up?
Yes, it is free, and no sign-up is needed. Nothing is uploaded: the calculation runs in your browser on your own device, and the numbers you type are not sent anywhere.

content.quick_answer: Salary sacrifice cuts your taxable income by the amount sacrificed, so you pay less income tax and Medicare levy. content.formula_words: Tax saved by salary sacrifice — in words: work out the tax on the full salary, work out the tax on the salary after the sacrifice, and take the second away from the first.

example_steps: Tax on A$100,000: income tax A$20,520.00 + Medicare levy A$2,000.00 = A$22,520.00.

faqs: What is salary sacrifice in Australia?

It is an agreement with your employer to give up part of your salary in return for a benefit, most often extra super contributions. The sacrificed amount is not counted as taxable income, so you pay less income tax and Medicare levy on it.
How much of the sacrificed amount reaches my super?

This calculator takes 15% off inside the fund, so A$10,000 sacrificed puts A$8,500.00 into super. That is the standard contributions tax rate. A higher rate of 30% can apply to very high incomes under Division 293, which this page does not cover.
Do laptops, phones and tools still escape fringe benefits tax when salary sacrificed?

No. From 1 April 2027, work-related items provided through a salary sacrifice arrangement are no longer exempt from fringe benefits tax. That covers portable electronic devices such as laptops and phones, computer software, protective clothing, briefcases and tools of trade. The ATO published this change on 7 September 2026.
Does salary sacrifice change my super guarantee?

No. Your employer still pays the super guarantee of 12% on your ordinary earnings. The sacrificed amount is extra, on top of that. Check with your employer whether the guarantee is worked out on the salary before or after the sacrifice.
What is the Medicare levy shade-in?

Low incomes pay no levy, or a reduced levy. There is no levy on taxable income of A$28,011 or less, then the levy is 10% of the amount over that line until it reaches the full 2%. This calculator applies that shade-in.
Is this an exact figure for my tax return?

No. This is an estimate only, not professional advice. It uses the 2026–27 ATO rates, leaves out offsets, the Medicare levy surcharge, HELP repayments and Division 293, and it cannot know your full tax position. Check the ATO before acting on a figure.

faqs: What is salary sacrifice in the UK?

It is an agreement with your employer to give up part of your salary in return for a benefit, most often extra pension contributions. The sacrificed amount is not counted as taxable pay or as pay for National Insurance, so you save both income tax and National Insurance on it.
Why do I save National Insurance as well as tax?
Because National Insurance is charged on the pay after the sacrifice. On a £60,000 salary the saving is £2,000.00 of income tax and £100.00 of National Insurance, which is £2,100.00 in total.
Does my employer save anything too?
Yes. Your employer also pays less employer National Insurance, at 15% on pay above £5,000 a year. Some employers add some of that saving to your pension, but this page counts only your own saving.
Does salary sacrifice affect my state pension or benefits?

It can. A lower salary can reduce pay-linked benefits such as statutory maternity pay or mortgage borrowing, and it can affect the National Insurance record if pay falls below the threshold. Keep your pay above £12,570 a year so the record is protected.
What if my salary is over £100,000?

Then the Personal Allowance tapers away by £1 for every £2 over £100,000, and salary sacrifice can restore some of it. This calculator applies the taper, so the saving shown already includes that effect.
Is this an exact figure for my payslip?

No. This is an estimate only, not professional advice. It uses the 2026/27 HMRC rates for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and it leaves out student loan repayments, pension tax relief limits and Scottish rates. Check HMRC before acting on a figure.

faqs: When does overtime start in the USA?

After 40 hours in one working week, under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Those hours are paid at 1.5 times the normal hourly rate. Some states add daily overtime rules on top, which this page does not cover.
When does overtime start in Australia?

After 38 ordinary hours in a week under most awards. The first 2 overtime hours are usually time and a half, and later hours are double time. Your award can set different rates, so check it before relying on the figure.
Does overtime count for salary workers?
Usually not. Salaried workers are often paid a fixed amount whatever hours they work, unless their contract or award gives overtime. This calculator is for hourly-paid work.
What if I worked less than the standard week?
Then there is no overtime, and the answer is $0.00. That is a real answer, not an error: you were paid for your ordinary hours only.
Is overtime pay taxed at a higher rate?
No. Overtime is taxed at the same rates as ordinary pay. A bigger pay packet can push some income into a higher tax band, but the overtime itself is not taxed at a special rate.

content.example_title: Worked example: age 45, 10 years, £600 a week
example_steps: Count back 10 years from age 45: ages 45, 44, 43 and 42 give 4 years at 1.5 weeks = 6 weeks.

You need at least 2 full years of continuous service with the same employer. With less than 2 years there is no statutory payment, though your contract can still give you something.

Because the weeks depend on the age you were during each year of service, not the age you are now. A year worked at 44 counts 1.5 weeks, while a year worked at 30 counts 1 week, even for the same person.

For redundancies on or after 6 April 2026 the weekly pay used is capped at £751 in England, Scotland and Wales. If you earn more than that a week, the cap is used instead of your real pay. The most anyone can get is £22,530.

The first £30,000 of a genuine redundancy payment is free of income tax. Any amount over £30,000 is taxed in the normal way. This calculator shows the gross amount before tax.

No. Northern Ireland has its own cap of £783 a week and a maximum of £23,490. This page uses the Great Britain figures of £751 and £22,530.

Yes. This is the legal minimum only. Many employers pay an enhanced package under the contract or a settlement agreement, and that can be much more than the statutory amount.

Length matters most. A long phrase of random words beats a short password with symbols. Aim for at least 80 bits: for example, 14 characters mixing all four character types, or 20 lowercase letters picked at random.

As long as the discount rate is above zero, the discount factor is above one, so dividing by it always gives a smaller number. The longer the wait, or the higher the rate, the smaller the present value.

faqs: What does the internal rate of return mean in plain words?

It is the yearly return an investment earns, once the timing of the money is taken into account. Money received early counts for more than money received late, because it can be used sooner. The IRR is the single yearly rate that makes all the flows balance out.
Why is the first cash flow a negative number?

Because it is money going out — the amount you invest. Later flows are money coming in, so they are positive. The calculator needs that minus sign to tell the investment apart from the returns. If the first flow is not negative, it shows a clear message.
What if the cash flows never change from negative to positive?

Then no internal rate of return exists, and the calculator says so plainly instead of giving a made-up number. For example, if every flow is positive, there is no investment to earn a return on; if every flow is negative, the money never comes back.
Can an investment have more than one IRR?

Yes, if the cash flows change sign more than once — for example, money goes out, comes in, then goes out again. In that case more than one rate can balance the flows, and this calculator gives the first one it finds. Most simple investments change sign only once, so they have one IRR.

ROI looks only at the total gain against the amount invested, and ignores when the money arrives. IRR takes the timing into account: money back early is worth more than money back late. The ROI Calculator on this site does the simple total-gain sum.

ROI looks only at the total gain against the amount invested, and ignores when the money arrives. IRR takes the timing into account: money back early is worth more than money back late. The IRR Calculator on this site does the timing-aware sum.

Margin divides the profit by the selling price; markup divides the same profit by the cost. For a cost of $60.00 and a price of $90.00, the profit is $30.00, the margin is $30.00 ÷ $90.00 = 33.33% and the markup is $30.00 ÷ $60.00 = 50.00%. Margin is always smaller than markup for the same sale.

Use margin when you want to know what share of each sale you keep, and markup when you want to set a price from a cost. For example, a 50.00% markup on a $60.00 cost gives a $90.00 price. Many sellers mix them up and under-price, so this page always shows both, clearly labelled.

Then the profit is negative, and so are the margin and the markup — the sale loses money. For example, a cost of $100.00 and a price of $80.00 give a profit of −$20.00, a margin of −25.00% and a markup of −20.00%. A negative result is a real answer, not an error.

The margin is still a real answer — 100.00%, because the whole price is profit. The markup is not defined, because it would divide by zero, so the table shows that plainly instead of a made-up number.

content.formula_intro: The payback period is the simplest break-even measure: how long until the money coming back has covered the money that went out. It assumes the same cash comes back every year:

It tells you how long it takes for an investment to pay for itself. A shorter payback means the money comes back sooner, which is less risky. It does not tell you how much profit the investment makes after it has paid for itself — for that, use the ROI Calculator or the IRR Calculator.

No. This is the simple payback: it treats $1,000.00 back in year five as equal to $1,000.00 back in year one. A discounted payback would allow for that, but it needs a discount rate. If the timing matters to you, check the IRR Calculator as well.
What if the cash coming back changes from year to year?

This calculator assumes the same cash comes back every year. If the cash changes, add the yearly amounts up by hand until the total reaches the investment — the year it reaches it is the payback year. The IRR Calculator handles uneven cash flows properly.

Then the investment never pays for itself, and the calculator says so plainly instead of giving a made-up number. The yearly cash must be above zero for a payback period to exist.
Is a shorter payback always better?

Not always. A short payback is safer, because the money comes back sooner, but a longer project can still earn more in total once it has paid for itself. Use the payback period together with ROI or IRR, not on its own.

content.formula_intro: A z-score turns a raw value into a distance measured in standard deviations, so values from different data sets can be compared on the same scale:

faqs: What does a z-score of 1 mean?

It means the value sits exactly one standard deviation above the mean. A z-score of 0 means the value equals the mean, a z-score of −1 means it sits one standard deviation below the mean, and a z-score of 2 means it sits two standard deviations above it.
What does a negative z-score mean?

It means the value is below the mean. For example, a value of 70 with a mean of 75 and a standard deviation of 10 has a z-score of −0.5000. A negative z-score is a real answer, not an error — it simply shows the value is on the low side.
Why is the standard deviation not allowed to be zero?

Because the formula divides by the standard deviation, and dividing by zero has no answer. A standard deviation of zero would mean every value in the data set is the same, so there is no spread to measure against. The calculator shows a clear message instead of a made-up number.
What is a z-score used for?

It is used to compare values from different data sets, and to find how unusual a value is. For example, a test score of 85 in a class with a mean of 75 and a standard deviation of 10 is a z-score of 1.0000, which can be compared with a score from a different test with a different mean and spread.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 4 decimal places. For example, a z-score of 0.33333… rounds to 0.3333. The same rule is used in the answer, the bar and the table, so the figures always agree.

content.question: What is the confidence interval for this sample mean?
howto: Type the sample mean, the standard deviation and the sample size, then pick the confidence level. There is no Calculate button — the answer appears as you type.
Read the interval in the result line, rounded half-up to 4 decimal places.

content.quick_answer: A confidence interval is the sample mean plus or minus a margin of error, where the margin is the z-value for the confidence level times the standard error. For example, a mean of 50 with a standard deviation of 5 and a sample of 25 gives a 95% interval of 48.0400 to 51.9600. Type your own figures above.
content.formula_words: Confidence interval — in words: divide the standard deviation by the square root of the sample size to get the standard error, multiply it by the z-value for the confidence level to get the margin of error, then add and subtract that margin from the mean.
content.formula_symbol: interval = mean ± z × (standard deviation ÷ √sample size)
content.formula_intro: A sample mean is only an estimate of the true mean, so the interval shows the range the true mean is likely to sit in. A higher confidence level gives a wider range:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard normal confidence interval for a mean, with z-values 1.645 for 90%, 1.96 for 95% and 2.576 for 99%. No outside data is used — only the numbers you type.
content.example_title: Worked example: mean 50, standard deviation 5, sample 25, 95% confidence
example_steps: Start with the figures: sample mean 50, standard deviation 5, sample size 25, 95% confidence.
Find the standard error: 5 ÷ √25 = 5 ÷ 5 = 1.0000.
Find the margin of error: 1.96 × 1.0000 = 1.9600, using the z-value for 95% confidence.
Add and subtract the margin from the mean: 50 − 1.9600 = 48.0400, and 50 + 1.9600 = 51.9600.
Answer: the 95% confidence interval is 48.0400 to 51.9600.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 50, 5 and 25, pick 95%, and the result line shows 48.0400 to 51.9600.
faqs: What does a 95% confidence interval mean?

It means that if the same sampling were repeated many times, about 95 out of 100 of the intervals worked out that way would hold the true mean. It does not mean there is a 95% chance that this one interval holds it — the true mean is fixed, and the interval is the estimate.
Why does a higher confidence level give a wider interval?

Because being more sure needs more room. The z-value grows with the confidence level — 1.645 for 90%, 1.96 for 95% and 2.576 for 99% — so the margin of error grows with it, and the interval widens. A 99% interval is wider than a 95% interval from the same sample.
Why does a bigger sample give a narrower interval?

Because the standard error is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. A bigger sample divides by a bigger number, so the standard error and the margin of error shrink, and the interval narrows.
What if the sample size is 1?

The interval cannot be worked out from a sample of one: a single value gives no sense of the spread, and the formula needs a sample size of at least 2. The calculator shows a clear message instead of a made-up number.
Does this assume the data follows a normal shape?

Yes. This interval uses the normal z-values, which suits a large sample or data that is roughly bell-shaped. For a small sample from data that is far from bell-shaped, the interval is only a rough guide — a statistics textbook or a teacher can advise on the right method.

content.formula_intro: The discriminant, b² − 4ac, decides what kind of answer there is: positive means two different real roots, zero means one repeated root, and negative means no real roots at all:
content.formula_source: Formula source: the standard quadratic formula. No outside data is used — only the three numbers you type.

faqs: What is a root of a quadratic equation?
A root is a value of x that makes the equation true — the value where the curve crosses the x-axis. For x² − 5x + 6 = 0, the roots are 3 and 2, because 3² − 5 × 3 + 6 = 0 and 2² − 5 × 2 + 6 = 0.
What does it mean when there are no real roots?

It means the discriminant is negative, so its square root is not a real number, and the curve never crosses the x-axis. For example, x² + 1 = 0 has a discriminant of −4, so the calculator says plainly that there are no real roots, instead of giving a made-up number.
What is a repeated root?

It happens when the discriminant is exactly zero: the plus and minus parts of the formula give the same value, so there is one root counted twice. For example, x² + 2x + 1 = 0 has the repeated root x = −1.0000.
What if a is zero?

Then it is not a quadratic equation at all — it is a straight-line equation, bx + c = 0, with one root. The calculator shows a clear message and asks for a value of a that is not zero, instead of dividing by zero.
How do I check the roots by hand?
Put each root back into the equation: the result must be zero. For x = 3 in x² − 5x + 6 = 0: 9 − 15 + 6 = 0. For x = 2: 4 − 10 + 6 = 0. Both check out.

It tells you how steep the line is and which way it leans. A slope of 2 means the line rises by 2 for every 1 it moves to the right. A slope of −1 means it falls by 1 for every 1 to the right. A slope of 0 means the line is flat.

It is the power you must raise a base to in order to get a number. Log base 10 of 100 is 2, because 10² = 100. Log base 2 of 8 is 3, because 2³ = 8. The log undoes a power, just as division undoes multiplication.
What is the difference between log base 10, natural log and log base 2?

Only the base changes. Log base 10 is the common log, used for scales like decibels. The natural log uses base e, about 2.718281828, and is used in growth and decay. Log base 2 is used in computing, because computers work in binary. This calculator does all three — just type the base.

Why can the base not be 1?

What is hexadecimal, and why do the letters A to F appear?

Hexadecimal is base 16, so it needs 16 digits: 0 to 9, then A to F for the values 10 to 15. It is used for colours on the web, memory addresses and file codes, because one hex digit stands for exactly four binary digits.
What is octal?
Octal is base 8, using the digits 0 to 7. It was once common in computing, because one octal digit stands for exactly three binary digits. It is less used now, but this calculator still shows it.

faqs: How do Roman numerals work?

Seven letters stand for numbers: I is 1, V is 5, X is 10, L is 50, C is 100, D is 500 and M is 1,000. Letters are added together, except that a smaller letter before a larger one is subtracted: IV is 4, IX is 9, XL is 40 and CM is 900.
Why does this calculator stop at 3,999?

Because the standard system has no single letter above M (1,000), and 3,999 — MMMCMXCIX — is the largest number that can be written with the usual rules. Larger numbers need a bar over a letter, which is a different system, so the calculator shows a clear message above 3,999.
What is the smallest Roman numeral?
I, which is 1. There is no Roman numeral for zero, because the Romans had no symbol for it. A number below 1 shows a clear message.

Because the subtraction rule is part of the standard system: a smaller letter before a larger one is taken away, so IV is 5 − 1 = 4. The calculator only accepts numerals written the standard way, and it says so plainly if a numeral is not written correctly.
Can I type lower-case Roman numerals?
Yes. The calculator reads lower-case letters the same as upper-case, so xiv works the same as XIV. The answer is always shown in upper-case.

Work out the social insurance: pension 9.3% of 60,000 = 5,580.00; unemployment 1.3% of 60,000 = 780.00; health 8.75% of 60,000 = 5,250.00; long-term care 1.8% of 60,000 = 1,080.00, so the total is 12,690.00.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 60000, and the result line shows €37,988.96.
faqs: What is a tax class?

Your tax class (Steuerklasse) tells your employer how much tax to take from your pay. Class I is for single people, which is what this page uses. Married couples use classes III, IV or V, and single parents use class II, so their figures are different.
What is the Grundfreibetrag?
It is the basic tax-free allowance: the first €12,348 of your taxable income in 2026 is taxed at 0%. Everyone gets it, and it is taken off before the tariff is applied.
What is social insurance?

It is the mandatory cover taken from your pay: pension, unemployment, health and long-term care insurance. The employee pays about 21% of salary in total, but only up to the ceilings: €101,400 for pension and unemployment, €69,750 for health and care.
What is the solidarity surcharge?
It is a surcharge of 5.5% on your income tax, but most people no longer pay it. In 2026 it only applies when your income tax is over €20,350 a year, and it rises gradually from there.
Does this include church tax?

No. Church tax is an extra charge for members of a registered church, usually 8% or 9% of your income tax depending on the state. It is not included here, so members pay a little more than the figure shown.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. Each line is rounded to cents first, and the take-home pay is the salary less those rounded lines, so the figures always agree.

What is the solidarity surcharge?

content.question: What is my take-home pay in Singapore?
howto: Type your yearly salary. There is no Calculate button — the take-home pay appears as you type.
Read the take-home pay in the result line, rounded half-up to 2 decimal places.
Check the bar and table under the result (Part 5 below) to see your CPF contribution and income tax.
content.quick_answer: Take-home pay in Singapore is your salary less your CPF contribution and your income tax. For example, on S$60,000 in 2026 the CPF contribution is S$12,000.00 and the income tax is S$1,110.00, so the cash take-home pay is S$46,890.00 a year. Your CPF money is savings in your own account, not lost pay.
content.formula_words: Singapore take-home pay — in words: work out your CPF contribution, work out the income tax on what is left after CPF, and subtract both from your salary.
content.formula_symbol: take-home pay = salary − CPF contribution − income tax
content.formula_intro: CPF is worked out on your salary, and income tax is worked out on your salary less CPF. The 2026 figures are:
content.formula_source: Country: Singapore. Year of Assessment 2026 (income earned 1 January to 31 December 2025). Source: IRAS and the CPF Board. Last checked 11 November 2026. This is an estimate only, not professional advice. CPF (employee, aged 55 or under): 20% of salary up to the Ordinary Wage ceiling of $8,000 a month ($96,000 a year). Income tax (residents): 0% to $20,000 of chargeable income; 2% to $30,000; 3.5% to $40,000; 7% to $80,000; 11.5% to $120,000; 15% to $160,000; 18% to $200,000; 19% to $240,000; 19.5% to $280,000; 20% to $320,000; 22% to $500,000; 23% to $1,000,000; 24% above. Chargeable income here is your salary less your CPF contribution. No other reliefs are included. CPF applies to citizens and permanent residents; Employment Pass holders do not pay CPF.
example_steps: Start with the salary: 60,000.
Work out the CPF contribution: 20% of 60,000 = 12,000.00.
Answer: the cash take-home pay is 60,000 − 12,000.00 − 1,110.00 = S$46,890.00 a year, or S$3,907.50 a month. The S$12,000.00 of CPF stays as savings in your own account.
content.example_note: Try it in the tool above: type 60000, and the result line shows S$46,890.00.
faqs: What is CPF?

CPF (Central Provident Fund) is Singapore's mandatory savings scheme for retirement, housing and healthcare. Employees aged 55 or under put in 20% of their salary, and their employer adds 17% on top. The money stays in your own CPF account; it is not lost pay.
Is there a ceiling on CPF?
Yes. CPF is charged only on ordinary wages up to $8,000 a month ($96,000 a year) from 1 January 2026, and on total wages up to $102,000 a year. Above those ceilings, no more CPF is taken.
Do Employment Pass holders pay CPF?

No. CPF applies to Singapore citizens and permanent residents only. Foreign nationals on an Employment Pass, S Pass or Work Permit do not pay CPF, so their cash take-home pay is higher than the figure shown here.
When do I pay my income tax?

Singapore has no monthly PAYE withholding for most employees. You file once a year with IRAS (usually in March or April for the previous year) and pay the tax as a lump sum or in 12 monthly instalments.
Are tax reliefs included?

Only the CPF relief is included: your employee CPF contribution is taken off your salary before the tax is worked out. Other reliefs, such as the earned income relief of $1,000, are not included, so your real tax can be a little lower.
How are the answers rounded?

Every result on this page uses one rounding rule: half-up to 2 decimal places. Each line is rounded to cents first, and the take-home pay is the salary less those rounded lines, so the figures always agree.

faqs: What is chargeable income?

It is the income your tax is worked out on: your salary less the reliefs you claim. On this page the only relief is your CPF contribution, so chargeable income is your salary less 20% CPF, up to the $96,000 ceiling.
What are the tax rates?
Residents pay 0% on the first $20,000 of chargeable income, then 2%, 3.5%, 7%, 11.5%, 15%, 18%, 19%, 19.5%, 20%, 22% and 23% in the higher bands, and 24% only on income above $1,000,000.
Do I pay tax every month?
No. Singapore has no monthly PAYE withholding for most employees. You file once a year with IRAS and pay the tax as a lump sum or in 12 monthly instalments starting in May.

Only the CPF relief is included. Other reliefs, such as the earned income relief of $1,000, are not included, and all reliefs together are capped at $80,000 a year, so your real tax can be a little lower than the figure shown.
What about non-residents?
Non-residents are taxed differently: usually a flat 15% on employment income or the resident rates, whichever is higher. This page is for residents only.
